The B^0_s meson, a particle composed of a bottom quark, an anti-quark, and bound by a force mediated by gluons, serves as an invaluable laboratory for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. Precise measurements of its lifetime and related oscillation parameters are essential for this endeavor. This article details the utilization of LHCb Collaboration data collected between 2010 and 2018 to perform time-dependent studies of decays into K^-_S K^-_S and phi phi final states. The research employs the "on-off" methodology, which contrasts the decay rates of particles with specific values against those that do not, while simultaneously assessing the CP-mixed averages. This approach aims to refine the precision of B^0_s lifetime determinations within the LHCb detector framework.

This study examines the origin of the centrality-dependent variation in the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$) by analyzing the influence of collision centrality on the average charged-particle multiplicity. We demonstrate that the significant change in $\langle x_{MCHC}\rangle$—representing the mean charged-particle transverse kinetic plus longitudinal kinetic energy per unit of rapidity—across different centralities drives a corresponding increase in the average transverse momentum ($\langle p_{T}\rangle$) for charged hadrons. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to enhanced binary collisions at more central (head-on) impact parameters. Furthermore, the work confirms that these hadronic effects adequately account for the observed rise in the central-to-peripheral ratio of the nuclear modification factor, $R_{AA}^{CP}$, within the energy regime of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC).

We demonstrate that noncommutative quantum mechanics on a constant, globally commuting momentum infrastructure can be interpreted as quantum mechanics with noncommutative position operators in a constant, globally commuting infrastructure. Specifically, by applying appropriate differential operators in the momentum area, we define the noncommuting position operators such that they satisfy the standard canonical commutation relations with the commuting momentum area. Furthermore, we prove the unitary equivalence between the standard quantum mechanical Hamiltonian defined by commuting position and momentum operators, and, assuming a time-independent Hamiltonian, its counterpart defined via these new noncommuting position operators. Notably, due to the global commutation of the momentum operators, the Hamiltonian in both formulations shares an identical spectrum. Finally, we derive the time evolution of expectation values for observables in both the position and momentum representations, showing that if an expectation value is initially computed using a function of commuting position operators, its time evolution mirrors exactly that of a function of noncommuting operators.

Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) serve as a critical prognostic indicator and potential target for therapies across numerous malignancies. Although pathologists traditionally assess these cells by visually inspecting digitized tissue sections, automating this quantification remains a significant hurdle. To address this, we created a dataset comprising 1,024 high-resolution (2.08 µm/lateral pixel) images of unstained, formalin-fixed, and paraffin-embedded tumor tissue sections from 51 melanoma and 51 breast cancer patients. These images were captured using reflected light microscopy after being stained with a fluorescence anti-DAPI antibody to highlight cell nuclei. We subsequently developed a specialized image analysis pipeline tailored to visualize these specific stained tissues. This method automatically segments nuclei, aggregates them into putative cells, and quantifies TILs while simultaneously removing common imaging noise, such as fluorescence background variability and out-of-focus blurring. Evaluations on an independent test set demonstrated a high degree of agreement between our automatic method and expert human annotations, with a Dice coefficient of 0.73 ± 0.09 and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 12.0 ± 2.5%. Finally, we applied this quantification to a multiparameter analysis of TIL morphology, noting distinct differences in nuclear size, shape, and TIL packing density between melanoma and breast cancer tissues.

This paper proposes a hybrid approach for soft-decision maximum-likelihood sequence estimation (SLSE) in optical communication systems. The method utilizes the feedback-enhanced sequence tracing algorithm, known as the modified Viterbi algorithm, to reduce memory requirements and boost error correction performance. The algorithm operates by jointly performing feedback-enhanced sequence estimation (WFE) and maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE). It starts with initial state metrics generated via the WFE algorithm, which are then refined through MLSE processing. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated under various feedback sizes, demonstrating that it maintains high performance even with small values. The results indicate a significant decrease in bit error rate (BER) compared to standalone WFE or MLSE alone, with feedback sizes of 2 and 4 showing superior outcomes relative to individual WFE and MLSE performances, respectively.

In deconfined strongly interacting matter, such as the quark-gluon plasma, event-by-event fluctuations in collision geometry induce corresponding fluctuations in hydrodynamic responses, including temperature, energy density, and momentum. This letter examines how such fluctuations affect heavy-ion collisions by analyzing their systematic behavior across center-of-mass energies and impact parameters, with a specific focus on proton-proton, proton-lead, and lead-lead interactions at the Large Hadron Collider. We find that these fluctuations are magnified by approximately an order due to energy dependence and are suppressed by a factor of ten via averaging among different system sizes. These results suggest that averaging measurement outcomes from varied scale system collisions—such as combining p-A, A-A, and pp results in pp-A mode—could significantly diminish flow fluctuations and thereby enhance the sensitivity to microscopic probes of quark-gluon plasma properties.

To effectively determine the initial correspondents within (DLE)-inductive terms, we introduce algorithm A (subscript L), an evolution of the method proposed by (D)LE. This algorithm is guided by the principle that the count of genuine, non-isomorphic first-order correspondents arising from such formulas is strictly bounded. We substantiate this hypothesis, establishing the algorithmial procedure for computing these correspondents. Furthermore, leveraging ALBA's efficient nature when handling initial correspondents, we present an upgraded version of the algorithm capable of managing these elements specific to (DLE)-inverse modalities.

Consistent Query Answering (CQA) stands as a pivotal research theme in Data Repairing, focusing on identifying correct responses by selecting plausible database states that align with certain views. View-CQA specifically seeks answers valid across all consistent data configurations preserving existing views. Recently, enhancing view-CQA performance has been achieved by integrating specific fragments of first-order logic (FOL). However, conventional methods face limitations when dealing with general cases, as they require over-approximating full view-CQA results for each individual formula fragment. This study introduces an innovative approach leveraging four-valued logic to derive view-CQA results directly for a broad class of FOL fragments. This proposed method demonstrates superior efficiency compared to existing techniques, particularly when processing complex queries that extend beyond the constraints of simple fragmentations.

Although linear models often serve as effective tools for modeling nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks due to their resilience, they frequently underrepresent complex time series patterns. To address this limitation, we propose a time-varying version of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (PARX) model. This TV-PARX model employs smooth functions to describe how autoregressive and exogenous coefficients evolve, allowing for gradual shifts. We further introduce an efficient estimation technique utilizing penalized spline methods with data-driven smoothing parameters selected via reparametrized minimum mean square error (MSE) criteria. Empirical analysis through a Monte Carlo simulation study demonstrates that the proposed estimator is consistent and achieves superior accuracy compared to rival models. Additionally, the methodology is applied to analyze the daily volume of new COVID-19 infections in the United States, illustrating the model's practical relevance.

Neural Descriptor Fields enable robots to master manipulation tasks by learning efficient representations of object affordances from very few demonstration examples. A critical step in this pipeline is automatically extracting robust 3D scene descriptors from raw point cloud data. We introduce a novel architecture for learning these descriptors from very few examples, ensuring they remain invariant to object pose and variations in texture while effectively encoding information crucial for task execution. To achieve this, we employ a learning framework consisting of two phases: initially, very few demonstration examples are used to train an object-specific feature extractor for individual items in a simulation environment, and subsequently, diverse stochastic data augmentations are applied during the inference stage to generate generalized descriptors that capture various positional and textural alterations. We validate the architecture against diverse real-world and simulated objects, demonstrating its ability to learn grasping and placing tasks from limited training data and successfully generalize to objects never previously encountered.

Addressing $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization on Cayley graphs with finite but unbounded degree, this paper investigates the complexity of low-temperature Glauber dynamics. We demonstrate that TAP-based update rules converge to produce an initialization for the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm, which subsequently recovers the ground truth with overwhelming probability in polynomial iterations. Concurrently, we establish that the TAP free energy functions as a Lyapunov direction for the standard AMP algorithm, thereby corroborating recent findings by Dong and Montanari regarding the existence of two distinct thermodynamic phases—replica symmetry breaking and replica symmetric—in the TAP free energy landscape within this system.

Metasurfaces supported by generalized sheet transition conditions (GSTCs) enable the modeling of three-dimensional electromagnetic interactions through a two-dimensional framework. These assets are essential for designing advanced metasurfaces that absorb electromagnetic energy efficiently and scatter it with full three-dimensional control. Nevertheless, existing efficient scattering operators capable of delivering complete control over the energy distribution are not without limitations regarding their implementation. This study introduces a strategy to mitigate these effects by substituting a single efficient absorption operator with multiple coupled operators across a stepped-index structure. Implementing this approach within a pencil-like geometry results in a performance performance that closely mirrors the theoretical ideal, as evidenced by a comparison of scattering efficiencies.

We introduce exPOTNN, an approach utilizing neural potentials trained with extended correlation potentials (ECPs) to model complex electron–nuclear interactions. These neural potentials are trained for systems containing one or two explicit atomic particles, where the actual particles are represented by effective particles with adjusted particle numbers, spatial correlations managed by one or two neural networks termed "space correlators." exPOTNN is trained systems exhibit a significant reduction in training data requirements, training time, and the occurrence of overfitting compared to standard training methods. Additionally, it enables the training of models that generalize to untrained atomic configurations and element combinations. This method facilitates rapid and accurate molecular dynamics simulations, including those involving molecular systems that incorporate newly added atomic species not present during the training phase.

We introduce a newly discovered large-scale structure in the nearby universe, known as the Giant Arc, which spans approximately 480 Mpc/composite units (Sloan/mega-composite units). This arc is oriented roughly perpendicular to the Sloan Great Wall and possesses a comparable root-mean-square density, yet its comparable linear dimensions suggest that the two structures together may constitute a single, colossal "cosmic string" encircling our local super-void with a radius of about 670 composite units. The formation of such a ring could potentially offer an explanation for why this surrounding void remains unfragmented despite its extensive size.

The TROPOmission mission aims to measure the vertical aerosol optical depth (VOD) across all of Earth, with a specific focus on the Antarctic Plateau. A key feature of TROPO is its wide-field radiometry, which allows for the determination of VOD without relying on strict absolute calibration. This is achieved by capturing the full sky diffuse daylight dome, where low-elevation light contains more aerosol-induced scattering than high-elevation views. Using radiative transfer modeling, this method calculates VOD by analyzing the relationship between measured radiance at different altitudes and the corresponding VOD values. This study utilizes data from the TROPO ground test stand to validate the algorithm, demonstrating its capability to determine VOD to within 0.005 even when absolute calibration is omitted. Furthermore, the research indicates that the accuracy improves to approximately 0.002 if the relative radiometric calibration is refined to 1%.

This paper introduces a method for object pose estimation that integrates local and global data to improve results in scenarios marked by heavy occlusion and clutter. Initially, a deep learning model generates a set of candidate poses by leveraging visual markers; subsequently, projected views of objects are utilized to cluster these estimates via a novel technique called "projection grouping." This process efficiently aggregates corroborating candidates into an accurate consolidated pose. Finally, an optimization algorithm refines the output by merging global and local information. Experimental results confirm that this approach achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This work examines the feasibility of detecting cracks in peridynamic models using kernel-based learning methods, focusing on peridynamic kernels with nonlocal horizons as a proxy for crack prediction. By leveraging a Fourier amplitude analysis of these kernels, we identify a monotonic relationship between a parameter $\alpha_0\in(0,1)$—which governs the kernel's shape—and the actual crack geometry. Leveraging this structural insight allows us to replace a standard learning task with an optimization problem aimed at minimizing error through adjustments to $\alpha_0$. Our results confirm that simplified family of kernels parameterized solely by $\alpha_0$ performs comparably to universally learned counterparts, provided the kernels adhere to specific physical constraints. Furthermore, we outline a generalized algorithm for constructing parametric kernel families under various constraint configurations to enhance efficiency.

This study examines various numerical algorithms for integrating Newton's equations of motion within classical molecular dynamics simulations, utilizing the alanine dipeptide molecule as a case study. As the system analyzed includes solvent molecules, an issue often overlooked in prior research, an examination of how integration precision influences both the conservation of total energy and the fidelity of computed physical and chemical properties is conducted. The paper offers comparative insights into the trade-offs among computational efficiency, numerical precision, and sampling quality inherent to different algorithms. Furthermore, it investigates whether certain methods are better suited for specific molecular characteristics, such as a stiff double-well potential found in biomolecular systems, and concludes that, contrary to common assumptions, certain numerical methods can yield superior results for certain molecular types.

The coalescence of binary black holes (BBHs) surrounded by matter generates distinctive signatures, including non-axisymmetric accretion disks, transient (or steady) asymmetements in emission, transient gravitational wave (GW) "chirps," enhanced GW radiation-driven evolution of the BBH orbits, and perturbations that allow astronomers to detect merging BBHs otherwise inaccessible through GW observations alone. While general relativistic simulations of such multi-body events are computationally prohibitive, this study investigates their dynamics using the (2+1)-dimensional, radiation-hydrodynamic approximation within the weak-field limit. We specifically examine how initial conditions—such as the orbital parameters, surrounding gas properties, and disk configuration—influence these orbital dynamics. Our findings indicate that surrounding matter can dramatically alter BBH trajectories, occasionally ejecting the system entirely, although these external influences generally do not dominate the timescales of event inspiral.

This work examines a specific class of linear time-invariant systems on a star-shaped metric graph, where the graph's boundary conditions are either Dirichlet or Neumann. The analysis establishes that, for these systems, the exponential stability rate is determined by the minimal distance separating the slopes' boundary conditions from conditions representing total elasticity. Furthermore, it demonstrates through a counterexample that elasticity parameters constitute the sole determinant of the exponential stability rate, implying that metric graph topology plays no such role. Finally, the method is validated against examples from positive networks with coupled elasticity conditions.

This paper describes the fabrication and acoustic testing of a Stycast 1090SI acoustic phantom. This stycast 1090SI phantom offers a radiologically transparent medium for medical imaging, allowing for the realistic simulation of tumors and other anatomical irregularities via embedded inclusions of varying acoustic properties. Impedimetric and attenuation measurements were performed on both the stycast 1090SI and reference plexiglass (PMMA) styrene polymer, with acoustic signals recorded using a hydrophone. Impedimetric results indicate that the acoustic impedance of stycast 1090SI approximates 1.40 x 106 ± 1% MRrayl, representing a 1% ± deviation from that of PMMA. Attenuation measurements revealed that stycast 1090SI exhibits an attenuation coefficient of 1.00 ± 0.05 dB/cm/MHz, which is 10% higher than that observed in PMMA. Additionally, the influence of titanium microtitan beads on the medium's acoustic characteristics was evaluated, demonstrating a direct correlation between titanium particle concentration and acoustic impedance. Finally, the study assessed how the stycast 1090SI medium affects the acoustic response of a piezoelectric transducer.

This study introduces a method to calculate node significance in multilayer networks that incorporates interlayer constraints. Our proposed approach is built upon the concept of node betweenness centrality and utilizes a quantum-regularized shortest path system with a solver based on a unified matrix formulation. We validate the accuracy of our model through comparisons with brute-force techniques under various constraint architectures, while also demonstrating its practical efficiency by reconstructing the interaction multilayer frameworks derived from significant node lists in both real-world data and synthetic scenarios.

This work examines the connection between the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime and the one in (anti-)de Sitter spacetime. It demonstrates that the Dirac equation in Minkowski spacetime can be derived from the (anti-)de Sitter version via a simple shift in the momentum operator. This approach aligns with the concept of twisted twisted equivalence. Notably, the derivation utilizes the algebraic framework of de Witt, employing the algebra of algebras of algebras. Furthermore, it is observed that the resulting Dirac equation in Minkowski spacetime incorporates interaction terms reminiscent of gravitational coupling, which is particularly relevant for exploring gravity-induced non-commutativity. Finally, an additional interaction is identified within the Dirac equation in Minkowski spacetime, which is attributed to gravitational coupling.

To address inquiries regarding causal structure analysis, the 'cdt' R package offers a collection of functions for building and manipulating models via a directed, reticulated visual representation. Leverage the 'magrittr' pipeline operator, `>%`, to chain commands efficiently throughout this workflow. The essential `cdt_graph()` function serves to instantiate data-based graphs, which can subsequently be expanded by adding observed variables using `add_node()` or direct input of an externally defined graph object. Removal of unnecessary elements is facilitated by the `remove_node()` and `remove_edge()` functions. Users can test for potential edge existence through `test_edge()` and visually render the resulting graph with `plot()`. Furthermore, the package is compatible with the `whatif` package, allowing it to effectively generate "What-If" scenarios directly within models. All `cdt` functions are fully vetted for integration into the comprehensive `vignette("cdt")` documentation.

Surface seals are integral to the functioning of most machinery, and understanding their behavior is vital for addressing issues like leakage, vibration, and premature component failure. This study examines how pressure reduction within the cavity influences surface seal behavior as impact velocity increases. Traditional modeling approaches typically assume the air film is fully aerated, a premise that fails during impact events where aeration is incomplete. To address this limitation, we developed a new theoretical model incorporating un-aerated film effects, which aligns closely with experimental data. Building on this, we created a comprehensive numerical simulation of the entire test rig, including the hydraulic cylinder, fluid, and structural components, utilizing it to forecast impact behavior inside the aerated chamber. Furthermore, we conducted physical tests to validate our numerical results, offering a robust framework for accurately simulating and predicting impact scenarios on surface seals.

We examine a specific class of charged states within quantum gravity, where the magnitudes of electric and magnetic charges adhere to the relation $|e|\approx |m|$. For these states, the spectrum is constrained such that $e \sim \mathcal{O}(n)$ and $m \sim \mathcal{O}(n)$, with $n$ representing an integer. We demonstrate that the entanglement first law generalizes Witten's effect, implying a minimum shift in a particle's electric spin of $\delta S \approx eB \equiv nB \approx nM_P^2$. Furthermore, utilizing the first law along with the weak gravity conjecture, we establish an inequality for the temperature $T$ of dyons:
$$ T \geq \frac{1}{2\pi M}\sqrt{e^2+m^2} $$
Finally, we prove that the weak gravity conjecture necessitates the existence of a particle violating the bound
$$ \sqrt{e^2/4\pi G + m^2/4\pi G} < \sqrt{e^2+m^2} $$
for some states, thereby confirming the conjecture.

To the original formulation of the Box Paradox, we supply a resolute solution by identifying the indispensable role played by the option to choose. Strikingly, this finding holds even scenarios where selection is impossible due to fatalistic constraints, ensuring selectivity remains a pivotal element in the resolution. Removing this aspect introduces an irreparable flaw; its elimination undermines the solution. The electronic structure of natural CuFe$_2$S$_4$ (cubanite) is investigated using the full potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the framework of density functional theory. This study addresses two key features of cuanite that other research has struggled to explain: first, the stability of its charge state as an antiferromagnetic insulator, and second, the occurrence of simultaneous charge ordering and ferromagnetism. Within standard DFT, neither the stable insulating state nor the charge-ordered state emerges. However, incorporating Bader charge analysis reveals that electron localization in the $3d$ orbitals of copper and the partial occupancy of a specific molecular cation ($Cu^{\text{I}}Cu^{\text{II}}S_4$) are critical. These mechanisms successfully model both the charge stability of the $Cu^{I}Cu^{I}Cu^{I}Cu^{I}S_{16}$ structure and the onset of ferromagnetic interactions.

We propose a quantum scheme that enables the realization of controllable Rabi oscillations and long-term coherent storage of light by simultaneously tuning the incident laser's frequency and the quantum dot's transition frequency to match either or both detunings of the acoustic mode. This control is exercised over the interaction between photons and phonons within a one-dimensional quantum dot (LD)-coupled acoustic cavity (CA). Specifically, adjusting the driving laser's frequency allows regulation of these oscillations and ensures sustained storage of photon states. Furthermore, reducing the coupling strength between phonons and phonons slows down the effects of noise. By minimizing this coupling, the adverse impacts of noise can be significantly mitigated. Collectively, these strategies promise robust operations for phonon-based quantum technologies.

A Hererringbone lattice serves as a versatile platform for simulating diverse tight-binding Hamiltonians, including the square, triangular, kagome, and checkerboard lattices, by incorporating checkerboard-checkered patterns that cancel out magnetic flux. We demonstrate that applying specific perturbations to the herringbone lattice allows for the realization of the triangular antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, which acts as the fundamental building block for numerous advanced quantum systems. Furthermore, we show that slight modifications to these perturbations result in the checkerboard antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, a parent lattice for the checkerboard neural-state model and other related quantum models. Although these perturbations introduce structural defects, the resulting lattice largely preserves key characteristics, offering a pathway to explore the impact of disorder on generated quantum systems within superconducting quantum annealers.

We examine the generation of Fock states surrounded by coherent amplitudes, known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs), via two methods: single-photon input into a quantum cascade of cascaded beam splitters (QS) or into a parametric amplifier (PA). The PA approach yields a distribution of outcomes that includes various numbers of photons, whereas the QS method isolates a pure state by detecting the photon in one specific output port. Comparing the two, the PA-generated state at full amplification mirrors the QS state but exhibits a broader range of final states due to higher variability in photon counts. Conversely, the two-step protocol offers a cleaner, pure-state result. Furthermore, regarding information retrieval, a full-strength PA allows for the extraction of a photon from an impure coherent state with greater probability than the two-step method applied to a mixed input state, where an photon extraction yields a pure-state outcome. Finally, in terms of utility, the non-classical attributes of the qs-derived pure-state SPCCS prove superior to those of the PA-generated states when compared across different strengthening levels, making the qs source more effective for quantum applications.

We express the complex Weyl tensor coefficients within the Newman-Penrose formalism as real 4-vectors, a reformulation that recasts gravitational wave physics in terms utilizing real quantities. Consequently, the transverse nature of these waves is now represented as an orthogonality condition involving Weyl tensor components relative to a Newman-Penrose null basis. This approach also enables the explicit real vector-based description of Gravitational Wave packets constructed through Huygens synthesis.

We introduce a framework to characterize evolutionary polymers, such as viromes and bacterial communities, by inflying their implicit "monomers" from data. Our approach relies on reconstructing the "oligomers" of these invisible monomers in the form of essential, irreducible interactions. We propose two techniques to characterize these high- dimension, low-valency oligomers: a Maximum Likelihood approach and a novel Annotated Interaction Graph (AIG)-based method. Together, they define an integrated pipeline for estimating the existence, number, and identification of oligomers for any irreducible interaction set suitable for representing the underlying monomers. We applied these methods to two complex polymers—an E. coli community and a SARS-CoV-2 virome—demonstrating that our models capture key structural features of the real system. Although developed for molecular data, this framework is applicable to any visible-to-invisible one-to-many mapping system defining an evolutionary polymer.

Dual patients sharing a single ventilator offers a method to reduce costs and alleviate machine shortages during a pandemic, yet it remains a challenging task to maintain the target tidal volume ($V_T$) when ventilating two individuals from one machine. In this paper, we present a solution that achieves a precise $V_T$ for both patients by utilizing feedback based on chest expansion. Our approach is built on a nonlinear state-space model of the respiratory system, which is parameterized using compliance and resistance values specific to each patient. We propose an algorithm to estimate these parameters online, enabling the system to adapt in real time. Furthermore, we implement a control algorithm designed to ensure the tidal volume targets are met. Experimental results from a bench setup and data derived from two clinical cases confirm the effectiveness of this strategy.

Dilated attention-enhanced Densely Connected U-Net (Dil-Dense U-Net) is a state-of-the-art deep learning architecture designed for medical image segmentation. Although it demonstrates significant potential for automating esophageal tumor (ET) segmentation in CT scans, its dependency on large annotated datasets poses challenges in the domain. To address this limitation, this study introduces Deep Learning with Dataset Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (DUDA), an innovative domain adaptation framework specifically tailored to refine such state-of-the-art models. By incorporating a density reconstruction loss, DUDA enhances feature alignment between source and target domains during training. Furthermore, by incorporating a cycle consistency loss, DUDA preserves structural integrity in reconstructed images. Crucially, the method requires no annotations from the target domain during the adaptation phase and necessitates only a small number of sparsely labeled examples for reference. Evaluations conducted on a dataset of ET-affected CT images validate that DUDA, when integrated with the Dil-Dense U-Net architecture, significantly outperforms multiple existing domain adaptation methods.

Lithium modeling plays a critical role in determining oil and gas field development strategies and investment decisions. Traditional methods for calculating lithium models are often time-consuming, which hinders real-time formation assessment. This study introduces a rapid and precise inversion framework for evaluating hydrocarbon lithium models, known as EnRML (Ensemble of Randomized Maximum Likelihood). The method integrates two core strategies: Ensemble of Randomized Maximum Likelihood (Ensemble EnRML) and randomization of randomized maximum likelihood (EnRML). First, the method randomizes the covariance matrix to generate an ensemble of model parameters, significantly accelerating the computation required for the standard EnRML approach. Second, the technique uses the EnRML results to refine the EnRML ensemble through the "EnRML of EnRML" approach, thereby improving the convergence of the inversion results. Testing this method against synthetic data demonstrates that the LM-EnRML approach effectively accelerates model convergence while maintaining high accuracy.

This paper analyzes the effectiveness of a recently proposed algorithm that determines satellite-based user location by fusing signal strength measurements with simulation data. The algorithm functions by iteratively calculating the distance between the true base station (BS) coordinates and those perceived on the basis of Received Signal Strength (RSS) using the log-normal shadowing model. The core mechanism involves identifying the mean and standard deviation of RSS values from simulations to filter out overlapping data points from real-world field measurements. The objective is to establish the distributional parameters of RSS under ideal and actual measurement conditions to derive the true Base Station (BS) coordinates through the algorithm. Research into Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers advantages to societies with multiple languages by deploying applications such as machine translation and MTPC across the globe. This paper introduces a system designed to automatically generate target-language paraphrases given a source sentence and specific language pair. This approach utilizes high-quality paraphrase data from open web sources to train a deep learning-based machine translation model with paraphrasing capabilities. By incorporating paraphrasing into the machine translation objective function, the study demonstrates improved paraphrase quality measured against paraphrase accuracy on paraphrase quality, exceeding current state-of-the-art methods.

Current image captioning standards show outdated relevance for native English speakers, prompting a need for better generation protocols, especially since image descriptions are critical for empowering the visually impaired via screen readers. This study evaluates existing protocols and introduces a new, rigorous grammar assessment protocol that pairs a human evaluator with an automated metric. Results reveal that even leading models fail to reliably achieve a high correlation with human judges under these new conditions, highlighting a significant necessity for improved reliability in human evaluation methods for caption generation.

This study calculates the bulk and surface energy loss functions for various tantalum oxide phases, specifically $\text{Ta}_2\text{O}_5$, $\text{TaO}_2$, and $\text{TaO}_1.8$, along with their corresponding surfaces. Our approach utilizes linear muffin-tin orbital (LMTO) methods within the atomic sphere approximation to model these loss functions while integrating local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. Comparisons with experimental data derived from electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) and x-ray reflectivity confirmations indicate that incorporating local field effects is crucial for accuracy. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that spin-orbit coupling significantly influences energy loss function calculations in these materials due to strong atomic number dependence and the presence of fully occupied $d$-bands in tantalum oxides. In an effort to assess the impact of electron correlation, we employed $U$ parameters ranging from 0 to 3 eV within the LMTO framework using the coherent potential approximation (CPA). Results indicate that while correlation effects modify the real part of the diagonal potential, they have negligible influence on the imaginary component of the energy loss function.

"This paper conducts a quantitative analysis of how news misinformation propagates online, utilizing a comprehensive dataset of fact-checked false news trajectories collected between 2016 and 2019. The study examines propagation patterns through a rigorous review of overy 11,000 comment sections associated with these trajectories, focusing on the geographic origins of spreaders and the structural characteristics of comment networks. The primary objective is to assess the extent to which recent contributors from distinct, real-world segregated regions access and share information regarding verified corrected false narratives. Our findings indicate a predominant 'Big Sort' phenomenon, where more than 80% of comments originate from comment sections within the same strict-segregated region as the initial poster, despite widespread availability of the misinformation and official fact-checks. This observation holds true even for content explicitly flagged with correction notices. Furthermore, the research highlights that the intensity of the Big Sort effect intensifies as the time elapsed since a news item's initial online appearance increases, a trend observed across fact-checkable false information."

While prior research has examined how demonstrations influence speech, extending these inquiries to include variations in task elements—such as audio instructions, subtasks, or error conditions—remains largely unexplored. This study investigates whether these variations influence the underlying meaning of speech acts during a multi-step task where participants instruct others on assembling furniture. Utilizing eye-tracking and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to observe subjects executing the task while undergoing scanning, we analyzed whether functional brain regions associated with specific speech concepts showed differential activation based on whether a subject performed well, succeeded after an error, or learned from another's mistake. Furthermore, we assessed if activation patterns varied when subjects performed the task themselves under successful or failed audio guidance, or if activation differed when subjects performed the task correctly after an error demonstration or observed an error made by someone else teaching assembly. Our findings indicate that subject performance level significantly influences activation in speech-related concepts across multiple experimental conditions, whereas the impact of specific task elements on these activation patterns was less distinct. Additionally, we observed activation in non-linguistic brain regions linked to concept processing that correlated with performance outcomes.

This work proposes a new algorithm for computing the infinite outwards approximation of an ordered tree within the context of regular tree languages. Unlike previous methods, this algorithm does not hardcode the tree's outdegree; instead, it is derived from the finite tree approximation of the corresponding $n$-ary tree for every possible $n \ge 1$. By combining these fixed-degree approximations as their least upper bound via a multiset multisum operation, the algorithm generates accurate approximations of equal height across infinite trees of arbitrary, unmatched dimensions. This direct enhancement to existing techniques for representing equal-height outputs facilitates, in turn, more effective approximations when used as components in broader, unequal-height tree structures.

We reformulate the problem of finding a ground state in quantum field theory (QFT) as an Euler-Arnold problem defined on an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. Building on this framework, we demonstrate that associated Euler-Arnold equations transform the optimization task into an equivalent problem involving Heisenberg equations of motion. These equations allow for the determination of ground states within an effective theory characterized by a finite-dimensional Lie algebra corresponding to the model's symmetries. As a practical illustration, we derive the Euler-Arnold equations specifically for $SU(2)$-invariant QFTs containing interacting two-level systems.

Testing frameworks designed to evaluate decision-making agents often rely on reward modeling to assess actions, a method that encounters significant challenges when applied to conversational domains due to the difficulty of quantifying conversation quality numerically. This repository introduces a testing tool tailored for virtual conversationalists that utilizes an objective metric termed "Topic Alignment" (TA). The approach evaluates actions by measuring the distance between the system's output and the set of semantically equivalent target responses. To validate the tool's efficacy, we conducted an experiment comparing alignment scores generated by the proposed method against human evaluations of alignment. Results indicate that the proposed technique achieves a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.428 against human judgments, surpassing existing objective benchmarks which yielded only 0.095.

The search for dark matter in the galactic plane is motivated by the possibility that it comprises low-mass, dark objects. We demonstrate that current and future wide-field all-sky surveys, such as LSST, will be able to identify 99.99% of Earth-mass dark matter candidates within the first 100 light-years (30.7 parsecs). We introduce a Heuristic Cross-lingual Memory (HCMC) framework designed to enhance low-resource machine translation via Neural Translational Memory. Current methods relying on bilingual translation memory are hindered by cross-lingual distribution discrepancies and the accumulation of erroneous memory entries, both of which degrade performance. To address this, we proposed a heuristic mechanism that dynamically retrieves cross-lingual memory entries based on distributional semantics. Furthermore, we introduced a Heuristic Correctional Translational Memory (HCMC) module that automatically detects and rectifies mismatches in existing memory entries to maintain high retrieval accuracy. All source-target memory operations occur within a unified cross-lingual vector space. Experiments conducted on multiple neural machine translation benchmarks demonstrate that HCMC significantly surpasses state-of-the-art translation approaches using external bilingual memory, particularly in scenarios with limited training data.

This work presents an alternative proof regarding the local local existence of smooth solutions for the Yamabe flow on a compact, smooth Riemannian manifold $(M, g_0)$ of dimension $n \geq 3$, starting from an initial metric $g_0$ for which there exists a constant scalar curvature. It further establishes the demonstration of the local parabolic convergence of the flow to a metric conformally equivalent to one with constant scalar curvature. The findings further demonstrate the uniqueness with respect to the class of initial metrics.

Existing few-shot learning approaches typically rely on a meta-learning framework to enhance performance by reducing the number of training examples required. However, existing methods often assume that both training and testing data are drawn from perfectly Gaussian distributions, an assumption that fails in real-world scenarios where datasets contain noise and outliers. Furthermore, the majority of these approaches lack a mechanism to adapt to the statistical distributions of test data. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework that integrates test-time meta-learning with distribution matching. This framework enables test-time meta-learning by adjusting the distribution of a test data's support set to align with that of the query sets. Additionally, the method is lightweight in terms of parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this framework achieves the highest performance across multiple benchmarks in 1-shot and 5-shot learning tasks within the settings of Image Classification and Retrieval.

User preferences are fundamental to the success of recommendation systems, yet accurately modeling aspect-based preference changes remains a significant hurdle. To address this, we introduce a new component called Gate-Adjusting Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE). This module adaptively recalibrates the significance of preference historical aspects, allowing user preference representations to evolve dynamically. Furthermore, to boost interaction precision between aspect embeddings and available user behaviors, we employ a multi-view aspect attention mechanism that integrates multiple facet views. Comprehensive evaluations on three standard datasets confirm that our model outperforms several state-of-the-art methods.

We present a strategy for evaluating medical image segmentation models trained on synthetic images against real, unseen MRI scans. The core premise posits that the selection of training data determines model performance ceilings, leading to an approach that estimates this limit byvirtually training a model on a mixture of synthetic and genuine MRI data. While initially formulated to assess segmentation models transitioning from low-fidelity simulations to high-quality MRI, the method is broadly applicable to any model trained on artificial data and tested on real, unseen datasets.

This study introduces a flexible framework for network-based multi-agent optimization problems, which encompasses various models such as weighted average consensus, extended consensus, and minimum finding problems with implicit constraints. Within this framework, the authors examine a class of distributed solutions characterized by continuous, single-step updates utilizing continuous, possibly non-linear functions. The research establishes necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring these solutions converge to their target set in both noise-free and noisy environments. Furthermore, the analysis addresses the specific case of linear multi-valued mapping finding, demonstrating that the approach in this context generalizes the well-known Jacobi method.

While NVMM (Non-Volatile Memory Management) file systems are well-established for non-persistent operations, the optimal approach for building one for Optane DC PMMs remains debated. These devices offer significantly higher bandwidth and latency performance compared to system memory, but they require the application to explicitly set and clear the device's write-back indicator. Given that modern operating systems lack native POSIX support for this indicator setting, an NVMM file system is necessary to abstract this detail. We introduce **NOVA-relaxed**, a pragmatic solution that utilizes these explicit mechanisms. By capitalizing on the PMM's exceptional performance for uncommitted data, our design allows applications to achieve a substantial increase in throughput for small writes that remain pending, with negligible impact on other workloads. Consequently, **NOVA-relaxed** delivers a **3.5x** performance boost for applications handling small, persistent write tasks by leveraging the device's full potential, while maintaining comparable performance for other operations.

This paper introduces a novel, data-driven approach to modeling rendezvous behaviors, built on an established multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics (MD) framework. To evaluate and compare model performance, we propose a rigorous statistical testing procedure. Applied to individual and group-level rendezvous data from 1,488 participants, our results indicate that the multi-agent MD framework outperforms alternative models in fitting data at both the individual and collective levels. Furthermore, the model successfully aligns with empirical observations across multiple metrics, effectively capturing key aspects of human rendezvous planning and execution, including the influence of social norms on these activities.

This study presents specific heat, electrical resistivity, and N\'eel temperature ($T_{\rm N}$) measurements for the $x=0$, $x=0.25$, $x=0.50$, and $x=0.75$ members of the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ series. The compounds exhibit antiferromagnetic ordering at $T_{\rm N}=13.5$, $17.5$, $21.0$, and $22.5$ K for $x=0$, $0.25$, $0.50$, and $0.75$, respectively, with the effective magnetic moments for Gd and Cm aligning closely with free-ion values of $7.94~\mu_{\rm B}$ and $7.18~\mu_{\rm B}$. A distinct anomaly appears in the specific heat of the $x=0.25$ compound at $T_{\rm m}=10.5$ K, occurring between the $T_{\rm N}$ and the maximum specific heat peak at $T_{\rm max}=8.5$ K. While this feature resembles a gamma phase characteristic in pure CmSn$_3$, its position relative to the magnetic transitions in the mixed compositions suggests it originates from local magnetic inhomogeneities rather than a genuine gamma phase transition.

Emerging spin ensembles within diamond, formed by P1 (or T) vacancies, offer promising avenues for solid-state quantum technology, yet their characteristic optical spectral diffusion poses a significant hurdle. In this study, we attribute the spectral diffusion of T center clusters to dynamic defects in diamond, specifically those lacking a third dimension in periodicity (2D). We demonstrate that isotopically enriched $^{12}$C diamond exhibits roughly a 50% reduction in this phenomenon compared to natural abundance diamond. Furthermore, correlating this effect with nitrogen impurities indicates that nitrogen vacancies contribute to the phenomenon, allowing for the creation of nearly stable (within 2 nm) quantum frequency comb sources via isotopic enrichment and nitrogen doping.

This study introduces a hybrid algorithm for tumor identification that integrates the Morphological Tools and Region Growing Technique. The proposed method initiates region growing by utilizing morphological operations to set an initial seed value. Leveraging the capability of region growing to incorporate adjacent pixels based on homogeneity criteria, the algorithm achieves more precise tumor detection compared to standalone morphological tools, while also benefiting from its capacity to handle varying boundary characteristics. Evaluation against several datasets confirms the algorithm's superior performance when compared to other standard methods.

This paper explores the circulant matrix derived from degenerate Bernoulli numbers and establishes their fundamental properties. It provides generalizations regarding the determinant, rank, and rank nullity of these structures, as well as an understanding of how they interconnect with Circulant matrices over finite Galois fields $\mathbb F_q$. Furthermore, the author introduces the concept of the degenerate Witt matrix and demonstrates the finding that the vast majority of invertible $n$-point circulant matrices constructed with these numbers form a specific subset of Witt matrices of the same order $n$.

This study introduces a randomized selection technique for choosing target stellar spectra, aiming to identify the most representative line lists for fitting. We evaluate this approach against a parametric method, with both strategies applied to convert raw spectral data into reduced versions containing only model lines. Analysis of the Coefficients of Determination ($R^2$) for various line intensities reveals that the Coefficient of Variation for the resulting radial velocities (RVs) achieved through randomization is 1.5 to two times lower than that of the standard selection, with the advantage intensifying as the line list expands. Unlike the inconsistent performance observed with the parametric method, the random_teque provides a consistent reduction in RV scatter across different observations. Furthermore, the study finds that the line list is most beneficial for weak spectral features; consequently, randomized filtering reduces radial velocity jitter most noticeably in stars with metallicities $[M/H] < -0.5$, utilizing effectively 3000 lines. Finally, the researchers demonstrate that any observed improvement in randomized RV precision stems from stochastic variability rather than a reduction in bias.

This work introduces Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS), a medium access control mechanism tailored for sensor networks. The primary objective of HRS is to reduce the hidden terminal challenge, a significant issue in such environments. In this framework, nodes are organized into distinct hierarchical groups. Transmissions are distinguished by two parameters: hierarchical range, which determines the distance nodes target, and sector, which defines the directional orientation of transmission. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced content-based recommendation systems, their performance remains suboptimal due to coarse-grained entity embeddings. Current Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems depend on word representation models, such as Word2Vec, to derive vector embeddings. A significant drawback of these models is their tendency to position antonyms near their target word in vector space when those antonyms appear with high frequency, which can interfere with various NLP applications. This issue is particularly pronounced in the financial domain, where terminology often has multiple meanings and the stability of financial terms is crucial; for instance, if "bullish" and "bearish" are embedded too closely, the nuance of market direction is lost. In this paper, we introduce a new set of financial-domain-specific anti-synonyms constructed using financial news data sourced from FinancialMiners.com. Furthermore, we propose an enhanced version of the Skip-gram model that incorporates an explicit anti-synymy relationship, extending the training process with an optimization phase which explicitly aligns anti-synym pairs to maximize their mutual distance. Experimental results demonstrate that these new vectors successfully increase the separation between a term and its anti-synym while preserving high similarity between the term and other associated concepts.

This work addresses wideband waveforms that integrate multiple narrowband (NB) waveforms. Introducing a flexible framework, it unites existing selection methods for wideband waveforming, specifically examining throughputs under both fairness and total system performance metrics. Two proposed strategies are detailed: a random approach and an optimized algorithm using a greedy method. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed fair-throughput and combined sum-throughput strategies outperform current state-of-the-art solutions.

This work proposes a new numerical approach for simulating Rayleigh-B\'enard instability within a fluid dynamics framework, where a fluid is confined between two horizontal plates subjected to a vertical temperature gradient. The derivation begins with the fully compressible compressible Euler and energy equations, incorporating the equation of state and the first law of thermodynamics. The derivation continues by applying the Boussinesq approximation, which involves linearizing the energy equation around a reference state to yield a new simplified form suitable for further analysis. The resulting system of equations is discretized using a discontinuous Galerkin method, with the fully compressible and energy formulations integrated directly. Numerical results are presented that demonstrate excellent agreement with established theoretical predictions and prior research.

In natural language, multiple derivation paths can exist for any given sentence; our own ambiguity arises from the cognitive limits of any single competent individual. While computational linguists address this by employing statistical models that model such ambiguity probabilistically, human interpretation remains less understood. This paper posits that human resolution of ambiguity is best viewed as a function of a single, unique competent speaker, analyzing how constraints on formal language theories apply to this context. We propose using a stochastic version of Parsing Expression Grammar (PEG) as a formal framework to connect human interpretation with speaker competence. Our results indicate that this model not only accounts for any sentence being interpreted as structurally unique but also accurately predicts the specific syntactic structure chosen for any given sentence, particularly by incorporating the frequency-based lexical statistics observed in actual language use.

A significant hurdle in multiagent learning is enabling agents to acquire strategies that avoid iteratively dominated actions by relying solely on agent-specific reward signals. We introduce a novel approach that leverages the intrinsic reward architecture of deep reinforcement learning to guide agents toward avoiding iteratively dominated strategies. Specifically, we propose a method that utilizes a shared, implicit reward representation learned by agents to identify and iteratively prune dominated actions. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of this concept through a mutual anti-aversion learning task within a cooperative framework, showing that even through a common hidden reward signal, agents can master the identification and avoidance of iteratively dominated actions.

This study examines the Suszland model incorporating rewiring dynamics to represent contact network evolution throughout an epidemic. Connections are initially established via an Erd\H{o}s--{S}os\ random graph, which evolves through a continuous-time dynamic process. Rewiring occurs continuously, defined by a removal rate for old contacts and an addition rate for new ones, which may depend on node degree or current epidemiological status. By utilizing type-representative methods, we derive conditions ensuring the model's final fraction infected aligns with predictions from the standard Suszland model on a homogeneous, well-mixed population. Specifically, we investigate the impact of rewiring dynamics, identifying that the final outbreak scale remains consistent with the homogeneous model if new contacts are limited primarily to highly similar individuals. Furthermore, we examine the transition interval between the epidemic's peak and its conclusion, finding that the duration lengthens as rewiring accelerates.

Although function approximation enables experience replay to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) in extensive task environments, it often introduces severe estimation bias when combined with policy gradient methods. Addressing this issue, we introduce the Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VRER) framework, which utilizes low-variance importance resampling to rectify data collected via RL. Theoretical analysis confirms that value-based algorithms under VRER yield consistent resampled datasets, whereas policy gradient algorithms under this framework achieve a reduction in estimation bias. Empirical results across diverse MuJoCo tasks validate the superiority of the VRER framework over standard importance resampling and existing techniques.

To facilitate the analysis of linearized reactive flow turbulence, a foundational modeling approach must be established. Observing that the linearized framework functions best with a simplified base state, this research aims to achieve that state using a combustion model. While previous work by Lin et al. (2019) utilized an average single zone model (Zhang model), this study evaluates three alternatives—eddy dissipation model (EDM), eddy dissipation concept (EDC), and the Zhang model—across three distinct scenarios: a turbulent, adiabatic, and stationary single flame, a pressure-driven shock tube with a reaction, and an explosive shock wave with reaction. Results indicate that the EDM aligns most closely with the linearized theory's requirements for modeling these base states. Finally, this research demonstrates that a reaction shock wave analyzed within the linearized framework, utilizing the EDM-based base state, yields prediction results consistent with high-fidelity direct numerical simulation data.

Extremely high-energy (UHE) photons in the cosmos typically interact with background radiation fields, initiating extensive hadronic ensembles known as hadronic showers. These events generate distinctive signatures observable in both total and differential cosmic ray spectra, potentially offering insights into the nature of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. We examine the effects of spatial inhomogeneities in both the magnetic field and the (redshift-dependent) Eddington ratio of the source on such UHE events. Our analysis demonstrates that these factors can generate a diverse array of multi-Petoe (10^15 eV) cosmic ray signatures. Specifically, we explore the case of "shocked" events, where a photon initially confined by one set of conditions becomes absorbed after structural changes, releasing its energy as a cosmic ray burst. This phenomenon is anticipated to manifest as a distinct step feature in the cosmic ray spectrum, observable by next-generation detectors like the AugerPrime and POEMEx experiments.

We investigate nonlocal gravity by deriving it from a specific Riemann curvature identity, establishing a new constitutive relation that links local terms with nonlocal terms. This formulation allows the theory to be expressed in a closed, modified form suitable for integration into observational analyses. Regarding observable quantities, the constitutive relation is explicitly formulated in terms of the Weyl tensor and the Schaefer tensor, enabling the derivation of a modified Einstein field equation through the Schaefer formulation. Additionally, we establish a modified energy-momentum tensor for gravity based on this new relation; although it lacks geometric interpretation, it can be incorporated into observational analyses alongside matter terms. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) serve as an essential mechanism for ensuring fault-tolerant distributed applications operate consistently across decentralized environments. Nevertheless, selecting the appropriate CRDT implementation for a specific use case often presents a difficult challenge. Consequently, there is a clear need for a design framework that enables developers to efficiently create new CRSDTs or configure existing ones to match particular applications, while maintaining consistency checks and performance. This paper formally introduces such a framework, which encompasses a computational model, programming languages for CRSDT implementations, and the logic to verify their consistent convergence. Designed with practical utility in mind, the approach features an automated proof assistant that facilitates the construction of novel CRSDTs and also assists in refining existing solutions.

Associations between protein mutations and specific Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) serve as a valuable resource for fine-matching genetic variants from genome-wide association studies (GWAS). While prior research has evaluated this linkage for GWANTS targeting the same protein complex, we investigate whether such associations extend to entirely different proteins across various traits. Analyzing 15.5 million exonic SNPs from the 1000 Genomes Project alongside 12,901 high-confidence human traits, we identify 3.3 million SNPs linked to at least one function annotated change. These SNPs are associated with 11,213.5 MWAS (11,213.5 MWAS), which themselves are associated with at least one trait. We further demonstrate that the likelihood of discovering these links differs by both the trait being examined and the specific SNP in question, indicating that the pressure of natural selection acting on a gene can influence which variants are most likely to be detected. Our resource offers a practical means to prioritize follow-up investigations for non-functional variants by utilizing evidence of phenotypic impact derived from structural biology and evolutionary data.

We propose a novel method for estimating the masses of millisecond radio pulsars by utilizing the total eclipsing (totaling both radio and X-ray absorption) X-ray observations from low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) that contain neutron star (NS) companions. The approach involves running forward simulations of the post-merger NS + white dwarf evolution to generate a synthetic population of NSs with varying initial masses, spin periods, and merger remnants. These simulations allow us to determine the current X-ray emission rates of NS LMXLs and estimate how their emission compares to the emission of total-eclipsing radio millisecond pulsars. We find a factor of approximately 1000 increase in the current number of observed NS LMXBs relative to the current population of radio millisecond pulsators in the Galaxy, suggesting an average mass growth per accretion event of ~0.15 M⊙. This result implies that the current population of NS LMXBs could account for up to 10% of the total NS population in our Galaxy.

This paper introduces a robust and efficient method for measuring one-dimensional velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{\rm 1D}$) in wide binary (WB) systems. The approach utilizes line-of-sight velocities of member stars, which are aggregated into a set of "lines" defined by the projected separation from the system's barycenter along the sky plane. A Gaussian fit applied to the binned velocity distribution of stars yields $\sigma_{\rm 1D}$ with a typical accuracy of 10–20%. The required number of stars depends on binned velocity lines; for instance, a dataset containing 1000 reliable stars and 100 lines results in just 7.5 independent systems. We demonstrate the technique using the Gaia-QuaBun survey data, which identified 4,600 wide binaries with projected separations between 1,000 and 500,000 astronomical units within the Galactic disk. Results indicate that wide binary members exhibit velocity dispersions approximately 10% lower than those of field stars, providing strong evidence for dynamical relaxation in systems with median separations of roughly 25,000 AU.

This work investigates the geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights within a congruence subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. By integrating the findings of [10] regarding the geometric modularity of algebraic weights with those of [1], we demonstrate that although geometric modularity for a set of algebraic weights within a specific level can be, and often is, inseparable, this property can nonetheless be transmitted to congruence classes of non-algebraic weights. Active molecules and complexes can undergo long-lasting coherences involving distinct conformations, distinct from those arising from environmental noise. These phenomena are driven by strong couplings between vibrational modes and electronic or nuclear spin states, a process that can be further amplified by an anharmonic potential energy landscape. Such features are anticipated to appear in systems like hydrogen bonds, ammonia within clusters, and polyenes. This anomaly allows for the persistent existence of vibrations-electronic coherences even at room temperature, surpassing the typical picosecond limits and potentially enabling utilization of vibrational energy on ultrafast timescales. This review investigates their generation, characteristics, and potential applications in extending the control of chemical reaction barrier tunneling through anharmonic vibrations coupled into multiple quantum states. This approach could facilitate the manipulation of reaction selectivity and accelerate reaction rates by an order of anharmonicities.

This study introduces a new framework designed to generate semetically diverse dialogue responses by integrating two key mechanisms: a rejection sampling process and a similarity filtering step. Rejection sampling enhances diversity by progressively raising a threshold for semantic similarity, while the subsequent filtering ensures practical utility by removing responses that are too close in meaning to one another. To measure semantic relatedness, we employ BERTScore, addressing the constraint of existing diverse training methods that are limited to a fixed vocabulary of retrieval candidates. Furthermore, to mitigate bias in BERTScore, we utilize a BERTScore variant computed on a diverse set of sentences. Experiments conducted on two dialogue datasets demonstrate that these approaches effectively enhance response diversity without compromising the overall quality of the generated dialogue.

Driver monitoring systems that automatically recognize eye and head gestures are increasingly integral to automotive safety, yet their efficacy is often hindered by the computational demands of processing live video streams in real time. To address this, the proposed framework leverages a two-stage strategy that drastically reduces the number of video frames analyzed. In the initial stage, a low-complexation model filters frames containing faces and predicts specific regions of interest (ROIs) for eye or head actions. Subsequently, a specialized neural network conducts precise action recognition exclusively using these targeted ROIs. By shifting the heavy recognition tasks to only forecasted interest areas, the framework achieves a substantial drop in latency and boosts overall robustness, allowing driver assistance features to operate reliably under real-time constraints.

The effects of rapid rotation on the critical curves for hydrogen ignition and thermonuclear runaways in brown dwarfs and low-mass stars are examined. In rotating bodies, centrifugal forces induce significant structural and thermal deformations, which in turn alter the ignition conditions; this study utilizes full-deformation structural and thermal models to determine these changes. The results indicate that for H-III objects, the impact of rotation is mass-dependent: in the lower end of the brown dwarf spectrum, centrifugal effects increase the minimum rotation period required for hydrogen ignition, whereas in the upper end, the minimum required rotation period decreases. Conversely, the minimum rotation speeds for hydrogen runaway events decrease across the entire range of brown dwarf masses when rotation is factored in. The minimum rotation period for H-III ignition drops to as little as 1.8 hours for the most massive brown dwarfs when rotational effects are included in the models. Additionally, the minimum rotation period for hydrogen runaway events reduces to approximately 2.4 hours for the same class of objects when rotational dynamics are incorporated into the calculations.

Most approaches to deep learning model score calibration ignore issues arising from imbalanced class distributions. However, a shift in our focus reveals that score calibration is highly sensitive to class imbalance. Existing methods, developed under the assumption of balanced classes, result in poorly calibrated outputs for imbalanced tasks. We introduce a new framework that links calibration metrics to the underlying class distribution, offering a comprehensive analysis of how calibration methods perform across both balanced and imbalanced settings. Furthermore, we propose an ensemble scoring technique that integrates multiple individual model predictions. Testing on six real-world medical image datasets demonstrates that our approach markedly improves calibration for deep learning models facing imbalanced data, without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

The transition from open to closed-loop feedback controls is essential for enabling bipedal robots to manage disturbances and generate natural gaits. Although human locomotion research has extensively mapped sensory mechanisms supporting balance, feedback strategies for robotic gait generation have received far less attention. This paper introduces an experimental investigation of a bipedal robot operating under full-state feedback control, utilizing a comprehensive approach to evaluate performance across all gaits. The performance metrics are defined by comparing closed-loop and open-loop gaits through a new metric termed "post composition error." This error quantifies the deviation of a closed-loop gait from its corresponding reference trajectory, which itself differs from any actual open-loop gait. By selecting reference trajectories that closely approximate open-loop behavior, the study evaluates performance on individual gait phases, entire cycles, and specifically on critical moments such as zero-moment points (ZMP) and co-rotation phases. Results indicate a performance degradation of approximately 10% to 20% in state and torque tracking when applying full-state feedback control. Furthermore, the study identifies specific stable regions within the system's state space where feedback control induces only minor deviations from the intended open-loop trajectories.

In this setup, a set of agents, each characterized by a specific skill profile, must allocate tasks drawn from a distribution of varying difficulties to maximize the long-term average reward. The proposed method establishes an allocation strategy grounded in the probability distribution of task challenges. Furthermore, it formulates the problem of determining the task challenge distribution as a multi-objective optimization problem. Current and upcoming electron-positron colliders, including the International Linear Collider (ILC), Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), Circular Polarized e+e- (CEPC), Superconducting e+e- (FCC-ee), and the muon collider, stand to significantly advance theoretical precision strategies. These advancements will involve refining quantum electrodynamics (QED) and mixed QED frameworks, as well as QCD and its mixed variants, to achieve a precision level of approximately 0.1%. Furthermore, such accuracy is contingent upon the systematic evaluation of systematic uncertainties. This report reviews the present state of high precision QED and QCD methodologies, while also highlighting essential areas demanding further development.

Privacy-preserving machine learning has attracted significant attention, especially following regulatory changes like the GDPR. Although vertical federated learning (VFL) has emerged as a primary approach for structured data collaboration, implemented attacks reveal vulnerabilities in current VFL protocols regarding information leakage and insecure adjustments. This study introduces two novel attacks: modification and injection. The proposed techniques are protocol-agnostic, effectively bypassing known defenses, and successfully expose sensitive modifications to VFL inputs and outputs. Specifically, we demonstrate that these attacks can accurately reconstruct private training data and create precise copies of ground truth labels with high success rates. Furthermore, we show that the proposed attack can determine modifications to the truth data with high precision. Moreover, the method is scalable, performing precise data reconstruction on up to 100,000 records in approximately 10 minutes. Our findings indicate that current VFL environments are highly susceptible to such threats, underscoring the urgent necessity for more secure and reliable protocols.

Random Fourier Features (RFF), introduced by Quoc Le in 2010, remains a widely adopted method for approximating kernel functions. Despite its feature dimension reduction capabilities, RFF often retains more features than initially required for maintaining prediction accuracy. Addressing this inefficiency, we propose Random Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a novel technique utilizing random block-diagonal Fourier kernels to generate RFF. Our findings demonstrate that utilizing PRFF enables more significant dimensionality reduction while maintaining or surpassing original RFF prediction performance. We validate these results across multiple datasets and k-values (where $k$ denotes the number of features) using predictive accuracy, clustering performance, and k-means convergence speed metrics.

Additionally, we analytically examine the theoretical properties of PRFF, proving that the covariance between two PRFF vectors can be exactly reconstructed via a k-fold k-times block-kernel averaging process. We further analyze the variance of this covariance estimator, showing that PRFF yields a variance proportional to $1/k$. Numerical experiments support these theoretical claims, confirming that PRFF not only enhances prediction accuracy, clustering efficiency, and k-means convergence speed but also superiorly maintains clustering performance metrics.
