This paper presents a general framework to establish local existence, blow-up, and asymptotic behavior for solutions to the semilinear Schr\"odinger equation with a complex, possibly unbounded, and restricted domain geometry, involving non-purely imaginary coefficients in the real part of the second-order term. Within this framework, standard classical blow-up proofs encounter minor technical hurdles due to the presence of the boundary; consequently, the resulting blow-up solutions exhibit the expected asymptotic dynamics. Additionally, we propose a novel classical blow-up criterion that subsumes most existing results while largely disreg intricate geometric complexities associated with boundaries; moreover, this new criterion yields a specific, pure power-law blow-up result for the cubic nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with Dirichlet conditions on the unit disk under real coefficients in the nonlinear term, demonstrating that general global or local well-posedness phenomena can still occur despite the inevitability of blow-up in certain scenarios.

This article introduces a theory of positive-characteristic commutative algebra grounded in characteristic-zero syntax. It suggests that treating these systems as genuine algebraic structures on computers enables the implementation of sophisticated computational tools, including analogs of the Lifting The Exponent Lemma and Hensel's Lemma. The author defines models for this valuation within the integer polynomial rings of computable number fields, utilizing them to devise algorithms that compute a "te" value within zero-characteristic algebras possessing an absolute valuation function, with experimental results detailed in the text.

The breakdown of the "sum rules of spectral weight" serves as a signature indicator for breaking particle number conservation and offers a diagnostic tool to trace the metal-to-insulator transition within strongly correlated systems such as Mott-Hubbard insulators. This study presents experimental photoemission data capturing the complete evolution of a correlated metal across its Mott transition, observing that the changes in the electronic density of states are strictly offset by corresponding alterations in the real ion lattice densities. Specifically, while low-energy spectral weight accumulates in Mott transition, it originates not from a shift in real-space atomic sites but is transferred directly from high-energy spectral weight, thereby adhering to the conservation of total spectral weight. Furthermore, while previous research attributed the initial emergence of correlated metallic behavior at high spectral energies, this work demonstrates that the associated low-energy spectral weight is generated from an intermediate-energy range, contradicting the notion that spectral weight is strictly conserved only as a total sum without regard to its energy distribution.

We demonstrate a functional link between quantum error correcting codes (QEC) and models of disorder in statistical mechanics. By applying a coherent-state path integral formulation to the stabilizer group of a QEC, we derive a classical statistical mechanics model characterized by a per-pauli error rate and two additional parameters. The selection of the code's stabilizers directly determines the resulting mechanical model; however, each model in the one-subsystem, two-qubit (1-2) family corresponds to an associated QEC. Notably, the 1-2 model exhibits a one-to-many mapping: every instance of its classical configuration generates a valid quantum error correcting code. This relationship offers a framework for systematically generating 1-2 stabilizer codes and provides methods to analyze quantum error correction capabilities through the lens of classical mechanical model properties.

This study focuses on the electronic properties of quantum-well structures built from monolayer and trilayer tellurene layers, oriented perpendicular to the crystallographic c-axis. By applying lateral strain to these tellurene quantum wells within $\mathrm{In}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$ barriers, we achieve a substantial non-trivial band gap ranging from 0.13 eV to 0.56 eV as the well width increases. This achieved gap is notably larger than that found in bulk tellurene. Our findings indicate that the band structure is highly sensitive to strain; specifically, compressive strain induces a $\Gamma$-band character, whereas tensile strain fosters a non-trivial character by elevating the energy of the $\mathrm{L}_{6c}$ state above the $\Gamma_{25^{'}}$ state. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the critical strain required to switch the band character at the conduction band edge is significantly lower for quantum-well configurations compared to bulk tellurene. These results demonstrate that strain engineering serves as an effective strategy for developing high-performance, tellurene-based quantum-well devices.

This study examines fluid flow in fractured porous materials, focusing on the development and application of a new upwind finite volume scheme built upon a combined single-domain double porosity model. In this framework, single-domain treatment applies to the macroscopic (bulk) porous region, whereas single-domain modeling of the microscopic fractures is augmented by an upwind finite volume scheme to capture pressure discontinuities across blocking fractures. These fractures are mathematically represented using a Dirac-delta function. The implementation of this scheme necessitates precise estimation of the Dirac-delta coefficient via a source term term derived from a simplified one-dimensional derivation. Theoretical analysis establishes the scheme's consistency, which is supported by a practical example demonstrating its ability to accurately represent blocking fractures. Furthermore, the work investigates the influence of these blocking fractures on Darcy velocity and solute transport.

We address the challenge of choosing a hypothesis from a set of candidates when facing uncertainty. To model this framework, we assign each hypothesis a corresponding utility value. Our proposed method utilizes Monte Carlo techniques to determine the optimal choice by optimizing expected utility. We further establish theoretical limits for distinguishing hypotheses within this model and introduce novel metrics to assess the quality of utilities for that purpose. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is not only computationally efficient but also highly aligned with existing bounds on decision performance.

This work utilizes the DFT-based HSE06 functional within the framework of the frozen-phonon method to investigate the structural and electronic characteristics governing the optical transition of ZnTe doped with Mn. Analysis reveals that the $^{6}A_{2}S \to ^{4}S_{42}$ transition follows a parabolic cross-stroke (PCS) trajectory, exhibiting a transition energy of 1.98 eV. By applying the Mott-Seitz model, this study determines that the nonradiative recombination process encounters an activation barrier of 1.2 eV. Our findings indicate that under a critical exchange interaction threshold, the optical stability of ZnTe:Mn is primarily contingent upon doping concentration and the local local environment.

We examine a $(1+1)$-dimensional field theory involving complex $U(N)$ scalar fields coupled to $U(1)$ gauge fields, where the gauge fields are constrained by first-order equations of motion derived from an auxiliary metric. The topological structure of the $N$-dimensional target space is determined by its non-vanishing homotopy groups: $\pi_2$ and $\pi_N$. Consequently, the model supports both topological solitons (skyrmions) and instability-prone kink solutions, which in turn yield non-trivial scattering amplitudes. Specifically, skyrmion interactions are found to be governed by both topological charges and dynamical charges arising from fluctuations around the classical equilibrium state. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that magnetic skyrmions exhibit a dependence on $N$ regarding their spatial extension and the magnitude of the dynamical charge. This charge is governed by the $(N-2)$nd homotopy group of the target space, reflecting its geometric complexity through the $(N-2)$nd homotopy group. As a result, for supersymmetric (SUSY) skyrmions, the mass squared is explicitly determined by the coupling constant and the trace of the auxiliary metric.

We present a high-performance, parallel electron-electron Coulomb integral evaluator designed for parallel architectures, specifically targeting MPI and OpenMP environments. This implementation demonstrates efficient utilization of multi-core systems across numerous nodes. While fundamental to many quantum chemistry methods, including Hartree-Fock (HF), the evaluation of these integrals is notoriously time-consuming, often becoming a major computational bottleneck. Although significant advances have been made in parallelizing these processes, further gains are difficult to achieve. In this study, we demonstrate that, contrary to expectations, our optimized Coulomb code yields substantial speedups in the overall HF framework using modern approaches like Automatic Task-Based Parallelism (ATB), such as KOKKOS. Our results indicate that ATB-based parallelization effectively converges electron-electron Coulomb integral loops within the HF framework, maximizing performance by fully leveraging available system resources.

This study presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of how structural and dynamical disorder interact to trigger explosive synchronization. Focusing on networks with nodes governed by phase oscillators coupled through a symmetric adjacency matrix subjected to stochastic perturbations, we identify the transition characteristic—an abrupt change in synchronization—driven by co-existing mechanisms of dynamical and structural disorder. We establish a clear connection between this phenomenon and the emergence of multiple stable states, demonstrating its resilience across a broad spectrum of disorder scenarios, including advanc-ing and retreating disorder both within adjacency weights and on node degrees. Finally, we outline the characteristic features of this transition, highlighting an elevated value of the reverse nucleation phenomenon, which quantifies the system's high metastability.

We introduce a methodology for analyzing measurements of the stochastic gravitational-wave background (GWB) that remain valid regardless of whether the signal originates from a single source or a mixture of multiple sources. In an idealized, noise-free scenario involving known instrumental characteristics, this approach recovers the distinct characteristics of these signals. When noise is present, this technique recovers the characteristic shape of any dominant heavy component of the GWB—defined as particles whose contribution peaks before, at, or shortly after their decoupling—provided they exhibit a distinct shape compared to the foreground. While it cannot recover the specific parameters of such particles, this limitation offers a strategic advantage: it enables the ANTHROGENICITY test for dark matter by confirming the existence of at least one uninstrumented (undecoupled) source in the GWB, a prerequisite for that form of dark matter detection.

Acting as helical swimmers, nature's microrheological agents can trigger diverse behaviors such as the snowman-like effect, which arises when their curved trajectory shifts from a loose coil to a tightly wound helix. In this study, we determine the conditions producing this snowman effect by analyzing the motility of ellipsoidal swimmers propelled by gradient forces in chiral fluids. Our methodology integrates the interplay between gradient-driven motion and hydrodynamic interactions, employing the Smoluchowski framework to derive the effective (observed) particle trajectories visible on macroscopic scales. Our findings establish that the snowman-like effect emerges from a continuous transition: particle motion shifts continuously from a simple coiled path to a pronounced three-dimensional helix as the particle's orientation aligns increasingly with its direction of movement. Furthermore, by manipulating flow parameters, one can control the helical pitch, thereby enabling tunable manipulation of self-propelled micro- and nano-robots designed in ellipsoidal forms.

This study examines the application of co-evolutionary genetic algorithms (CGA) within peer-learning frameworks, employing a binary string representation where the objective function incorporates a metric for Hamming distance from a Nash Equilibrium. Expections of this equilibrium are modeled through two individual learning frameworks. Anticipating that social learning enables more effective convergence toward a Nash Equilibrium than private learning, we investigate the use of diversity maintenance operators to accelerate convergence toward specific target solutions. Introducing a specific bit-flip operator that inverts bits only when an individual holds the maximum Hamming distance from its current non-dominated set, we utilize these mechanisms to drive convergence toward the target. Experiments with various parameters indicate that, within a social learning framework, this diversity maintenance drives the population to the Nash Equilibrium in roughly $O(\log n)$ generations. In contrast, under individual learning conditions, the algorithm requires $O(\sqrt{n})$ generations to locate the Pareto front within a constant factor of $\sqrt{n}$; consequently, co-evolutionary genetic algorithms achieve superior performance compared to individual learning scenarios.

This study presents an automated framework for identifying and classifying cybersecurity threats within news sources to support risk mitigation. These insights are vital for maintaining system integrity and ensuring continuous operations. We propose a two-stage approach: first, utilizing a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with a Conditional Random Field (CRF) layer to extract Named Entities (NEs) and Key-Value-Pair (KVP) associations from text; subsequently, employing a Random Forest classifier to detect Specific Webspells-of-Attack (SWA) based on these structures. This method addresses the challenge posed by the absence of large, annotated public datasets containing NEs and KVPs associated with security incidents. We introduce such a dataset, the News Security Incident Dataset (NSID), comprising 1,000 articles from the SEC's EDGAR database. Evaluations indicate that the model achieves a macro F1 score of 0.73 for NE and KVP extraction, and 0.83 for identifying SWAs, offering a practical, cost-effective, and automated mechanism for gathering critical security intelligence directly from public data.

This study examines a formation model incorporating magnetic interactions between agents holding distinct opinions. In this framework, every individual possesses a specific magnitude of opinion, and interaction strength varies based on the disparity between two opinions. By employing the mean-field approach, we derive a comprehensive mean-field equation capable of addressing any opinion distribution. Our analysis reveals that average magnetization follows a power-law scaling relative to the interaction parameter, with its exact exponent determined by the chosen distribution shape; specifically, magnetization consistently exceeds that of a conventional Ising model adhering to the same density, regardless of the distribution. Furthermore, long-standing dynamical patterns are successfully forecasted for specific opinion profiles, including a phase transition to an active state, which occurs even when total consensus magnetization reaches stability. Finally, our proposed field allows for the reconstruction of the complete temporal history of opinion dynamics.

For a broad spectrum of inverse and ill-posed problems, traditional solution methods often demand an explicit formulation of the problem operator, along with meticulous tuning of hyperparameters. In contrast, neural networks offer a flexible approach to such challenges, enabling the creation of solutions that are operator-agnostic and largely independent of specific hyperparameter configurations. This work introduces a method to train such general-purpose networks using a simplified loss function built upon a Bayesian framework for deconvolution. These models are then demonstrated to effectively solve related tasks, including image superresolution and the unfolding of compacted images.

We introduce a new technique for uniformly scaling input dimensions and another for scaling them with specified thresholds to enforce non-homogeneous input constraints within neural networks. Although these control strategies are widely adopted, prior research offered no analysis of their ability to prevent implicit input constraint violations in the input activation space. We address this gap by first examining input activations under an arbitrary constraint, establishing a corresponding transformation in the required weight parameters to establish theoretical bounds for these restrictions. Subsequently, we analyze the proposed scaling and threshold methods, investigating the conditions under which they effectively prevent constraint violations. Our approach involves comparing the transformed weight parameters against a corresponding theoretical threshold. Results indicate that the effectiveness of these range restriction methods relies on specific criteria, allowing us to derive explicit, necessary and sufficient conditions for the uniform scaling method and corresponding criteria for the partial input activation scaling method. Finally, we present numerical examples that validate our theoretical framework.

In modern financial systems, payment netting stands as a critical tool for enhancing both stability and efficiency by reducing the total volume of transactions required to settle obligations. However, as these systems expand in complexity, traditional graph algorithms often prove inadequate at identifying optimal netting outcomes within large, intricate web of economic interactions. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel adaptive data structure specifically engineered to resolve netting problems more effectively across diverse scenarios. By leveraging innovative decomposition and recombination strategies, this structure delivers significantly tighter runtime bounds than existing algorithms. Our approach caters to various netting variants by accommodating diverse order relations and scoring functions, with experimental results demonstrating its exceptional performance, particularly when processing real-world data.

We introduce a new approach for automatically tagging country and language names using only the associated flag as context. This method targets high-resource and high-performance outcomes in both low-resource and low-resource language identification. It improves existing techniques by leveraging external knowledge sources, including Wikidata entries, Wikipedia links, and language definition links from Wiktionary. These links are integrated into name-tagging models via a new auxiliary task designed to identify unique identifiers for each country and language. Experiments conducted across three groups of languages categorized by the number of available name-tags demonstrate that these findings are generalizable. Specifically, results for groups B (medium) and C (low) languages show a 2% absolute improvement in F1 scores over current state-of-the-art methods.

This study analyzes particle production across varying transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) ranges in diverse center-of-mass energy and collision system sizes at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). A distinct $p_{\rm T}$ dependence is observed in particle ratios for all systems, yet the specific value of $p_{\rm T}$ where the transition occurs from single- to multi-particle regimes shifts systematically with increasing system size. Furthermore, the work examines single-particle $p_{\rm T}$ spectra and nuclear modification ratios ($R_{\rm AA}$) to isolate the influence of system size, identifying that while the particle ratio-driven shifts account for the majority of structure in small systems, residual features persist in both the spectral shapes and $R_{\rm AA}$ distributions.

Noisy Labels exist across almost every major Multi-Woman Dialogue State Tracking (DST) dataset, yet current top-tier models ignore them and process data as if perfectly clean. Since these models rely heavily on noisy metadata—specifically Multi-Word Expressions (MWEs) and slot values—this study introduces two novel architectures designed to handle label noise. We evaluated these models against three dominant DST benchmarks, discovering that while existing top performers achieve high scores by simply overlooking noise, our approaches yield superior results when utilizing inherently noisy training labels. Furthermore, we identified that the inherent ambiguity of MWEs and slots in noisy datasets is a primary driver for the performance gaps seen in current top models. Finally, a proposed simplified DST framework, which also benefits from the effects of label noise, matches or surpasses the performance of all other models tested on these benchmarks.

We propose a novel framework for investigating how the spatial arrangement of a city's infrastructure affects the evolution of civil disobedience. By integrating a modified Suszlinn-Velzki model with a fractional Laplacian term that parameterizes spatial mobility, we examine the resulting Frankl-Laszevi equations utilizing a variational approach. Our analysis within a variational setting reveals the existence of solutions exhibiting both stable and mobile patterns of revolt. Finally, we apply these findings to an urban road network to illustrate specific instances of localized and disseminated rebellion.

Using the Prospector Bayesian inference framework, we assess the reliability of derived star formation rates regarding the star-dying timescales associated with ionizing photons. This methodology incorporates the star-dying timescale ($t_{SFH}$) as a free parameter within a grid of stellar population synthesis models, which are then constrained by ultraviolet (UV), optical, and near-infrared (NIR) spectral energy distributions (SEDs). This constraint utilizes both the main-sequence star mass-luminosity relation and the $\chi$-distribution of ionizing photons. We evaluate this approach on a UV-to-NIR Prospector template based on a mock galaxy catalog containing 10,000 objects spanning redshifts $0.5 < z < 2.5$. The results indicate that the new method recovers the true star-dying timescale ($\tau$) for star-forming galaxies, though it overestimates $\tau$ for passive systems. This overestimation is likely due to dust attenuation and the effects of a stellar halo. To gauge the accuracy of the star-dying timescale estimation, we utilize $\chi$-distribution of ionizing photons as an independent metric. To establish a fully symbolic decision procedure for verifying regular expression containment, we utilize the standard tool of the Brzozowski operator along with integration over the space of all possible string monoid homomorphisms. Current implementations of this approach are inefficient because they operate within an unrealistically large state space of morphisms; consequently, we introduce an optimized sub space that effectively resolves this issue. Limiting computation to this adjusted subspace yields a decision process capable of handling regexes with approximately 100,000 symbols—representing more than an order of magnitude improvement in capacity compared to prior methods.

Current vision-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms leveraging deep learning utilize end-to-end neural networks to extract environmental features from IMU data and camera streams more efficiently than conventional methods. Nevertheless, these advanced VIO systems are hindered by significant feature mismatches between stereo and monolithic sensor setups. This study introduces a new monocular VIO framework built on a unified, reversible, and stereoscopically configured network architecture. By employing three artificial cameras in a stereo arrangement, the proposed system achieves a 3D scene representation that the original image-taking single camera cannot provide on its own. Through a carefully engineered training methodology, the model ensures consistency in depth perception across all three artificial cameras in this stereo setup. Additionally, the training process aligns these generated 3D features with corresponding inertial measurements to produce precise global poses. Experiments conducted on both real-world and simulated datasets demonstrate a marked improvement in performance relative to current state-of-the-art solutions, while the system maintains high efficiency in terms of both speed and memory consumption.

This work introduces the concept of square-root topology within a low-energy effective model for higher-order Weyl semimetals (HWSMs), which are characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of surface Fermi arcs and bulk Fermi nodes. These three-dimensional HWSB can be viewed as an extension of both the simple Weyl semimetal and the hybrid scenario. At low-energy approximations, the formation of bulk Fermi point results from the intersection of a set of mutually orthogonal, pairwise HWSBs. At a specific critical parameter, a pair of Weyl points emerges; this pair can be traced back to the coalescence of four triply-degenerate triple points, which themselves originate as pairs of creation/annihilation of the hybrid scenario. These findings are substantiated by the topological charge structure and confirmed via angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy simulations of the relevant surface states. The provided model and its parameter-dependent behavior offer a roadmap for engineering materials exhibiting this square-root topology and for distinguishing them from other higher-order HWSB configurations.

This study examines a model involving $s$ missing data measurements across a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ with an smooth boundary, where the observed data outside $\Omega$ and the remote measurements outside $\Omega$ are known. The model incorporates a long-range interaction term representing data measured at a distance, specifically formulated as $\int_{\Omega} u(x)(R_\Omega[u](x))^s \, dx$, in which $R_\Omega[u]$ denotes data accumulated on the boundary $\partial\Omega$. We present the numerical solution using edge finite element methods. First, we derive the convergence of this scheme by establishing the well-posedness of the model and analyzing its convergence characteristics. Next, we detail the process of discretizing the remote data-at-a-distance operator and prove the numerical resolution's convergence. Finally, through various numerical experiments, we validate the theoretical findings and investigate how the algorithm behaves when incorporated with a data-priori weighting parameter.

Grid cells, discovered in the rat medial entorhinal cortex, are renowned for generating hexagonal spatial fields that have long served as a cornerstone in theories of brain-based navigation and spatial representation. Growing evidence indicates that these cells also react to non-sensory cues; even minor shifts in visual, auditory, or olfactory inputs can alter a grid's phase or configuration, causing the entire overlay to shift laterally or rotate. While prior research has analyzed how pairs of grid cells react to translational shifts using probability distributions, this study focuses on modeling the activity of triplets of grid cells in response to small rotations. We demonstrate that a carefully chosen set of orientation-dependent phase relationships allows a single, unified metric to localize rotations with high precision. Our findings indicate that grid cell triplets function analogously to diad pairs, serving as highly sensitive detectors for subtle environmental rotations.

We utilize a global dynamo model to investigate the genesis of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars through kinematic dynamos. Our numerical simulations solve the mean induction equation on a spherical shell, incorporating Coriolis forces and anisotropic turbulent diffusion. Results indicate that cycles emerge when these rotational and diffusive forces interact to sustain magnetic activity even in the absence of a magnetic tachocline, a mechanism we attribute to the alpha-omega dynamo. We determine that cycles in such stars depend critically on the rotation rate and the differential structure of diffusivity. Specifically, we find that cycles persist under weak rotation provided that diffusivity is highly differential, for instance, if it is restricted to the convective envelope. By analyzing these systems, we conclude that cycles offer insights into the internal magnetic generation mechanisms of rotating stars with complex convection zones, such as the Sun and solar-type stars in later evolutionary stages.

We examine the dynamics of irreversible entropy production across a broad spectrum of quantum quenches in non-equilibrium systems, utilizing two distinct models: the transverse Ising chain and the mass Bessel step potential field theory. Our findings indicate that for mass-quench scenarios, both initial and final temperatures govern this entropy change irreversibly, a conclusion supported by a universal scaling behavior. We further observe that for systems where the mass steps linearly with time, the irreversibility of the entropy change is minimized. By linking these results to the emergence of an effective temperature, we derive an upper limit for irreversible entropy production that is consistent with universal scaling. It is important to note that this bound is surpassed when the mass-quench is abrupt at the onset, whereas for quenches that are linear in time, the predicted universality holds.

We examine how non-unitary dynamics evolve when considering an initial joint state of a system and its environment. Demonstrating a functional connection, we show that the time at which system-like decoy dynamics emerge—referred to as the distinguishability time—is determined by the period of time-twirling the initial state with respect to system unitary dynamics via the system's characteristic timescale. Furthermore, we illustrate that the magnitude of system-like decoy dynamics within this non-unitary framework is inversely related to purity under the corresponding time-twirling evolution on the system and setting. These findings offer fresh perspectives on understanding non-unitary dynamics, specifically by elucidating their inherent dependence on the system's initial environmental correlations.

Interpolation problems with minimal energy are addressed using a set of nodes in the unit cube $Q_n = [0,1]^n$. It is confirmed that a nondegenerate regular simplex with vertices in $Q_n$ and minimal potential $U_\alpha$ (of order $\alpha$, where $0 < \alpha < n$) exists provided $3 \le m \le N_n$, where $m$ represents the count of such nodes forming this optimal regular simplex with the potential value equal to that of the simplest regular simplex sharing the same potential. It is further demonstrated that for $\alpha = 1$ in dimensions $n=2$ and $n=3$, this most energetic-avoiding configuration corresponds to a specific well-known geometric structure. Additionally, $M_n$ is explicitly defined as the largest integer $m$ for which such an optimal regular simplex can exist within the cube.

This study compares the plasma etching of silicon oxide layers on silicon wafers with the direct etching of silicon. When plasma etching silicon directly, the resulting carrier concentration reaches $10^{19} \text{ cm}^{-3}$, whereas etching through a buffer oxide layer yields a concentration of $10^{18} \text{ cm}^{-3}$. The lower impurity levels observed in the buffer oxide scenario are attributed to reduced sputtering rates of silicon compared to sulfur-containing contaminants introduced during the process. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of varying etching times on the structural integrity of silicon, finding that a 10-minute etch preserves the silicon lattice, while extending the process to 30 minutes results in the formation of silicon nanocrystals.

Modeling atmospheres solely through external forces like stellar irradiation is insufficient; a coupling between a planet's interior and exterior is equally vital. We present a comprehensive modeling study of this interior-exterior dynamics for tidally locked super-Earths possessing thick atmospheres. Our work integrates two key models: a 1D radiative-convective atmospheric simulator and a thermal evolution interior code. The latter solves the heat equation in a multi-layered setup, incorporating phase-dependent volumetric latent heat release from the core crystallization to the overlying crystallization. Our framework simulates heat transport via both adiabatic convection and efficient insulating plates stabilized by a magnetic insulation effect.

The primary goal of our research is to investigate how atmospheric and internal conditions evolve and interact over time. We specifically address the question of whether a stable, locked state is always attainable, or if certain orbital configurations trigger persistent oscillations as heat cycles between the interior and exterior. Our analysis reveals that these super-Earths can exist in multiple distinct states—ranging from fully molten worlds to those with strong magnetic fields and extreme atmospheric conditions—dictated primarily by their distance from their host star (orbital semi-major axis) and initial thermal configuration. Furthermore, specific orbital setups can induce oscillatory behavior in both the atmosphere and the deep interior as they cycle heat between layers. These dynamics are crucial because they can alter a planet's observable characteristics, such as spectral signatures and the morphology of cloud features.

This study examines the interaction of various propylene oxide (PO) isomers with hot surfaces, focusing on ionization mechanisms relevant to the formation of toxic methyl cations ($CH_3^+$) in low-pressure combustion systems. Using hot surface ionization (HSI) mass spectrometry, researchers analyzed $1,2$- and $1,3$-propylene oxide ($1,2$-PDO and $1,3$-PDO). Results indicate that $1,2$-PDO produces significantly more methyl cations than $1,3$-PDO; this difference is attributed to the necessity of C–C fission for generating $CH_3^+$ from $1,3$-PDO, a pathway hindered by the high thermal energy required. Furthermore, introducing $1,2$-PDO enhances $CH_3^+$ generation from $1,3$-PO by approximately 20%, a phenomenon explained via electron capture-detachment fluorescence (CDF) and the creation of surface-bound intermediates. These findings offer a foundation for further investigation into identifying ionizable compounds within combustion systems and quantifying their concentrations.

Recent developments have independently established a bidirectional correspondence between variational parametrized quantum circuits and training via gradient descent on loss functions. Building on this foundation, our work addresses the issue of loss function selection by introducing a novel approach that leverages the representation of tensor networks within parametrized circuits. We demonstrate this by applying standard loss functions to train tensor network representations of the Heisenbard Hamiltonian across one and two dimensions. Our findings indicate a performance improvement of roughly a factor of 10 compared to existing methods, with negligible additional computational overhead.

Deep learning techniques, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), have demonstrated significant efficacy in addressing complex medical challenges, including cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. Although much of the recent literature on clinical graph neural networks relies on the availability of detailed annotations to construct graph data, this constraint frequently hinders their development and deployment. This study introduces a novel transfer learning framework designed to elevate the performance of GNNs in cancer research by adapting models trained on graph structures from alternative domains to represent tissues and anatomical features within medical imaging datasets that share similar modalities but lack specific image-level annotations. To validate this framework, we developed and utilized two distinct graph representations derived from CT scans of mice and humans, serving as sources for transfer learning. Consequently, we adapted state-of-the-art GNN models trained on these representative graphs to classify ten distinct tissue types using a target dataset, such as contrast-enhanced CT scans from patients at a single-institution setting. The experimental results indicate that this framework successfully achieves a mean accuracy of 68.1% across the tissue classification task. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that sharing latent image-level semantic features through comparable anatomical graph structures from different tasks or species enables effective task-specific performance, even when the target task involves limited data.

Multivariate point processes, characterized by their ability to model complex interaction patterns among diverse event types through varying inter-event intervals, have found extensive applications in domains such as neuroscience, seismology, and financial economics. Although a traditional linear framework known as the linear Hawkes process has become standard, it falls short in representing nonlinear dynamics. To address this gap, we introduce the linear threshold Hawkes process, which utilizes these capabilities while maintaining sufficient statistical tractability. We have established consistency and asymptotic normality for parameter estimation using maximum likelihood methods and developed a novel nonparametric intensity inference technique based on the linear theory. Performance of these methods has been validated via Monte Carlo simulations and practical case studies, involving intracranial EEG spike data and S&P 500 stock returns data.

Segmenting medical images poses a challenge, particularly when labeled data are scarce. Although contrastive semi-supervised learning (SSL) has shown promise in natural scene analysis, its application to medical imaging is hindered by anatomical variability across scanners and institutions, which creates domain discrepancies that degrade segmentation quality. Additionally, the requirement for multiple labeled samples per object type to train effective contrastive semi-supervised models exacerbates this issue, making acquisition difficult. To address these challenges, we propose Consistent and Strong Cyclic Cyclic Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA), a novel framework designed specifically for contrastive semi-supervised segmentation across different anatomical settings. Our method introduces a cyclic domain adaptation mechanism that iteratively enhances mutual information between a target domain and a source domain using consistent feature alignment using cyclic domain adaptation (CS-CDA). Specifically, the method aligns features from the target domain with those from the source domain through cyclic domain adaptation (CDA), ensuring that mutual information remains consistent across domains. Additionally, we implement a multi-view data augmentation strategy that generates diverse perspectives of the same anatomy to create robust cross-domain representations. To address labeling scarcity, we further develop Consistent and Strong Cyclic Domain Adaptation (CDA), which improves feature alignment by reducing the need for extensive annotated datasets through cyclic domain adaptation techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves segmentation accuracy, achieving an Dice coefficient improvement of 3.33% over the baseline CS-CDA method.

To establish the BRS symmetry within the first-order formalism of $D=3+1$ supergravity, a suitable gauge-invariant action is first constructed. Building on this foundation, it is demonstrated that proper comprehension of supergravity using the 3+1 first-order formalism relies entirely on a rigorous treatment of BRS symmetry in this specific formalism, rather than merely the 3+2 formalism. Within this framework, the anticommutator of two local supersymmetry transformations in the 3+2 formalism is derived in a standard fashion. In contrast, an anticommutator generated by two local supersymmetries in the 3+1 formalism cannot be obtained directly. To resolve this limitation, two additional anticommutators generating diffeomorphisms in the 3+1 formalism are derived by first applying two local supersymmetries orthogonal to each other and then acting with a combination of one local supersymmetry and the corresponding diffeomorphism generator. This approach yields two distinct diffeomorphism generators, allowing for a linear combination that reproduces the expected result found in the 3+2 formalism.

This study introduces the concept of a plasma-based waveplate designed to mitigate the effects of Faraday rotation in radio interferometers. The device relies on differential group delay between left- and right-circularly polarized waves generated by the plasma's interaction with strong magnetic fields and leverages polarization conversion within a region containing varying electron densities. The required physical thickness of this waveplate is derived, a parameter that scales with the square of the electron density and inversely with the strength of the parallel magnetic field. This design utilizes electron density gradients created by a plasma stream from a de Laval nozzle, generated by an incoming magnetized coronal loop.

We evaluate the application of deep learning methods for weak gravitational lensing, a critical component of cosmological analyses that utilizes image distortions from galaxy distributions to extract information about the majority of matter in the universe. A primary example is weak lensing (WL) lensing mapping, where a full set of three-dimensional dark matter halos is inferred from one-dimensional radial average density profiles. We contrast two neural network architectures—an Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and a Universal Approximator (UA)—to assess their ability to model the mapping function. A Residual Network (ResNet) is employed to enhance the performance of the MLP by incorporating prior knowledge. Results indicate that both neural network approaches significantly outperform traditional estimators. Specifically, the UA achieves performance gains of 2 to 3 times over the standard estimator, while the MLP demonstrates improvements ranging from 1.5 to 2 times. Furthermore, performance with the ResNet approach improves by approximately 50% when utilizing prior information. These enhancements are particularly significant in the context of dark matter profiling, where the performance of the standard estimator is already near its theoretical limit.

Furthermore, it has been established that a single segment identification is achievable when $\theta$ traverses a full $360^\circ$ rotation ($0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$). The research also indicates that rotating the system by $90^\circ$ in increments of $\theta$ enables identification of individual segments within a single image frame. Practical validation was conducted by simulating images generated during a $360^\circ$ rotation at a $90^\circ$ step, utilizing a camera to record the image intensity as a function of $\theta$. These simulations confirm that the identified segment corresponds accurately to the actual physical segment activated at each rotation step.

Acquiring labeled data is often costly, yet most supervised learning approaches depend heavily on it. Selective labeling offers a viable solution by strategically choosing the most valuable samples for annotation to maximize label efficiency. However, existing selective labeling methods frequently fail to recognize that only a subset of these samples is actually required to achieve the desired model performance. In this paper, we introduce a new framework called Self-Memory Selective Labeling (SM-SL). This system automatically identifies which data instances have reached sufficient proficiency through self-assessment, thereby determining exactly how many external labels are needed to reach the target accuracy. Contrary to traditional models that use a fixed threshold for stopping data collection, our method dynamically adjusts the selective labeling criteria based on ongoing self-evaluation. We tested SM-SL across three distinct datasets featuring diverse data distributions. Results demonstrate that the framework significantly lowers the number of labels needed while maintaining a target accuracy of 1%, compared to fixed-threshold baseline methods.

The merger of two neutron stars generates both gravitational and electromagnetic radiation, with the latter offering a means to detect these events through wide-field optical and gamma-ray telescopes. If the resulting neutron stars are sufficiently massive, the collision will produce a black hole, yielding a source of strong gravitational waves that can be observed by next-generation detectors like Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer. Such sources are expected to occur at a rate of roughly one per cubic parsek near Earth, translating to approximately 100 events per year within a Milky Way-like galaxy. This study investigates the signatures of such neutron star-black hole (NSBH) mergers in the electromagnetic spectrum, focusing on electromagnetic counterparts arising from magnetosphere interactions and the formation of short-lived, magnetized accretion disks. We find that the timescales for a test particle to orbit around a spinning black hole are significantly longer than the timescales for magnetic field line reconnection, a discrepancy that could explain the absence of observed outbursts in some NSBH mergers. Additionally, we estimate that upcoming wide-field optical and gamma-ray surveys will be capable of identifying electromagnetic signals from roughly 10% of these NSBH mergers annually, while X-ray observatories may detect about 30% of them.

Social determinants of health (SDOH) represent critical influences on patient well-being, yet clinical documentation often lacks sufficient detail regarding these factors to support effective management and research. This study introduces an automatic named entity recognition (NER) system designed to identify SDOH within electronic health records (EHRs). The proposed framework utilizes the Mallet software for probabilistic modeling, with features based on feature-based word weighting. The model was trained and assessed using a dataset of 1,700 de-identified pediatric EHR notes, focusing on 10 specific SDOH categories. The resulting annotation set was constructed by 12 public health experts and divided into features using feature-based weighting. The resulting model achieved an F1 score of 0.7441. The study found that 9 out of 10 SDOH categories were successfully identified with an F1 score exceeding 0.7441. This study examines a swimmer confined to two fixed locations within a flow field that it can manipulate. The field features two stable states connected by a transition frequency, which an external agent can set at will. The agent selects how often the system switches between these states, and there is a specific expense linked to repositioning the swimmer from one stable state to the other. The objective is to minimize the total cost, balancing both the time elapsed and the effort expended for switching, to effect the swimmer's transition. The model incorporates both switching duration and switching effort to model real-world scenarios like magnetic particles, DNA molecules, and colloids in non-equilibrium systems. The results indicate an optimal non-trivial switching frequency that balances the trade-off between waiting time and switching costs, and the minimum total cost increases with the swimmer's potential energy barrier. A quantitative analysis is provided for a magnetic particle subjected to alternating magnetic fields supporting two stable configurations.

Urban encounters serve as indicators of city life's variety, frequency, and distribution across diverse spaces. Although pandemic-related restrictions significantly disrupted these interactions, it remains unclear whether lingering behavioral shifts will alter their long-term patterns. By utilizing high-frequency mobile data from 2019, 2020, and 2020, and analyzing travel purpose, distance, and urban functional zone classifications, this study reveals that the pandemic permanently altered daily routines, leading to a lasting decline in travel diversity. Prolonged remote work and sustained reductions in public transport and recreational activities drove these lasting changes. Furthermore, the pandemic dampened community resilience in adapting travel patterns, resulting in diminished diversity and stability. Prolonged confinement appears to have caused these outcomes, with policy recommendations necessary to help restore urban travel variety and stability.

The presence of migrants within circumstellar discs can significantly alter inner disc structures, particularly near the outer boundary of the active region of a high-mass young stellar object (HSO). This study examines such interactions in systems containing an HSO and its companion, utilizing three-dimensional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations to analyze how the induced disturbances extend to the innermost disc regions. Our findings demonstrate that migrating objects create substantial local clearings and ripples, a phenomenon that is more intense near discs aligned in coplanar configurations. Specifically, an opening of merely $5^\circ$ in the discs' mutual inclination can damp these effects by a factor of 10 to 100. The simulation results further indicate that migrating bodies generate inward-propagating density waves capable of altering specific angular momentum and generating sufficient gas drag to force the object's inward migration. Additionally, the thermal timescales of inner discs are found to be notably short, a factor that contributes to the formation of the observed inner disc holes.

This paper introduces a novel analytical model for 5G cellular exposure grounded in building attenuation physics. The approach accounts for 5G frequency bands, directional beamforming, and varying building types to address inter- and intra-cellular exposure, as well as risks from both small and large base stations. The paper's original contribution lies in the use of three-dimensional (3D) building geometry for cellular exposure analysis, moving beyond conventional two-dimensional (2D) footprints. This new model calculates the probability distribution of received power at any specific point within a building to offer a more realistic representation of actual exposure. The proposed framework was validated using real-world building data from New York City, with results benchmarked against existing literature. Additionally, the study estimates total cellular exposure based on 5G backhaul configurations and 3D urban mapping, offering a foundation for evaluating 5G network planning and construction strategies. Our analysis reveals that 5G base station exposure is exponentially lower than pre-5G levels due to building attenuation, with the majority of total city-wide exposure stemming from small cells. Furthermore, the research indicates that exposure levels are only marginally affected by the density of 5G towers, suggesting that optimal 5G planning can be achieved with minimal exposure monitoring.

This work addresses the free surface water wave issue within a horizontal, unbounded domain. Assuming the flow is irrotational and irremovable, we demonstrate a method to recover the surface shape by analyzing the envelope of the wave pattern. This result extends an earlier finding by Saut and Zuily, generalizing it beyond the limitations of low regularity. Our approach leverages the connection between the envelope method and backstepping control techniques, adapting their framework to a free boundary setting where the domain changes.

This study introduces a hierarchical control architecture designed to enhance a mobile platform's navigation, leveraging a set of sonar sensors for environmental perception. The lower layer functions as a direct interface with the actuation system, utilizing a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller to compute linear and angular velocities based on the discrepancy between current and target distances and orientations. The upper layer governs obstacle avoidance, path tracking, and mission execution; it determines the goal positions for the bottom tier by integrating data from multiple sonar inputs. This high-level logic employs artificial potential fields to manage obstacles while using fuzzy logic to refine its decisions based on how closely the vehicle follows a predefined trajectory. Experimental outcomes confirm the system's efficacy across various operational scenarios.

Detecting fake news is increasingly vital in an era where misinformation spreads rapidly and undermines social stability. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for identifying fake news that integrates contextual data. While many researchers argue that performance can be achieved using only textual content, we demonstrate that incorporating external context significantly enhances results. Specifically, we developed a context-augmented BERT model fused with an attention-based sequence labeling architecture. We sourced contextual datasets from FactCheck.org and Snopes.com to train and evaluate our system. Furthermore, we investigated the efficacy of adding varying types of contextual news. Our findings indicate that context integration boosts F1 scores by 4.31\% and accuracy by 2.75\% compared to models relying solely on text, with multi-type context achieving a total 5.06\% f1 improvement over text-only baselines.

This paper examines the decoding order selection problem in multi-user full-duplex (FD) non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) systems where the base station simultaneously transmits and receives signals. Under the assumption of perfect channel state information and binary modulation, the objective is to maximize the system's sum rates. Due to the objective function's non-convexity, as well as coupled integer constraints and non-continuous variables, the problem is resolved via a proposed suboptimal policy. This policy incorporates two heuristic approaches: the variable elimination method and a decoding-order-specific user element-wise mapping strategy. Building on these elements, complex computational hurdles are circumvented. Consequently, the selected decoding order is determined within a timeframe independent of the total number of users, thereby ensuring constant-time $O(1)$ complexity regardless of system scale. Simulations confirm that this suboptimal policy significantly enhances overall system performance by delivering superior sum rates compared to conventional optimal strategies.

To address rotationally invariant L1-PCA when dealing with data clusters, our approach introduces a two-step methodology. First, it generates multiple reparameterized views of the input dataset via rotation. Second, it solves the two-block transformation of this two-step process. Although the first step acts as a heuristic for generating annotations, the entire framework is grounded in a rigorous three-variable change-of-variables derivation that yields a three-algorithmic solution to its two-stage optimization problem. This first formulation achieves the established limit of multiple linear projections identified by d'Aspremont et al. (2007), while a subsequent, more streamlined algorithm offers practical implementation. This latest technique surpasses the original limit on sparse PCA performance, showing a preference for sparse loadings that enhance within-group betweenness.

Annotated datasets are fundamental to training supervised deep learning models, yet defects in the annotations propagate to the models and hinder overall performance. Traditional methods for identifying errors rely on computationally expensive computational checks or heuristic rules, which are often inadequate for tackling the complex problems typically found in computer vision tasks. This paper introduces a novel technique to enhance semantic labeling by using paraphrase tasks to detect and correct inconsistent label assignments. The approach involves analyzing neighboring sentences to find paraphrases of the current image description; any image elements that appear between these paraphrased sentences are then flagged for review. We evaluated this method on the MS-COCO dataset, which showed a significant reduction in both false negatives and false positives compared to baseline methods.

A prefix-independent half-positional winning condition allows for an algorithmic solution to the game, as all but a finite number of bits can be addressed algorithmically by shifting resources. While many standard conditions like reachability, safety, and their combinations are half-positional, this paper investigates whether the closure property holds for these conditions by asking if uniting prefix-independent half-positional conditions always results in one. We demonstrate that if an arbitrary conjunction of such conditions is considered, the result remains half-positional; however, disjoining two conditions can yield a non-half-positional outcome only if the first condition is strong enough to force the winner in any play, essentially determining the victory regardless of the second. A stronger query asking for the smallest non-zero fractional cost (as a 1-uniform vector) whose 1-uniform combination yields a non-half-positional condition is resolved by showing the answer is the irrational irrational number $\phi-1$.

Fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems are resolved here using a coupling strategy that divides the domain into individual structure and fluid parts. Within this partitioned framework, the solid and element-based calculations are handled separately from the fluid and element-based calculations, with data exchanged between them via data exchange methods. Although both problems are solved independently within their respective domains under this approach, findings are integrated to facilitate fluid and solid solutions. This study examines fluid and structure problems where displacement is constrained to specific movements. It is demonstrated that, provided the fluid remains stable under strong formulations using the Navier-Stokes equations with a Barotropic law, the proposed framework yields stable results for fluid and solid systems. Furthermore, a numerical example involving a fluid flowing around a flexible beam substantiates these theoretical conclusions.

To address the challenges of designing and debugging global navigation policies in expansive environments, we introduce HiTMap, a novel hybrid metric map built from interconnected tile-based elements. Unlike traditional global metric maps that demand creation and learning across entire environments, HiTMap captures the morphology of complex structures within a compact representation, thereby reducing population efforts and easing policy development through visual inspection. We propose learning the required motion primitives using reinforcement learning, which effectively generalizes across varying parts of the map. Validation through experiments in synthetic and real-world settings confirms that the system delivers rapid convergence, robust generalization, and seamless integration when populating new environments.

This paper details the development of LUMTS 2023System, which participated in Task 1 focused on identifying and classifying abusive Twitter content into Ingroup, Outgroup, and General categories. For its primary task (Abusive Tweet Classification), the team achieved a Macro F1 score of 61.4%. Relying exclusively on publicly available resources, the system utilized only the General training subset from Task 1 in LumTS 2022, as all other datasets were excluded from training due to licensing restrictions. To maximize the use of these constraints-compliant data, we implemented data augmentation strategies. The core architecture is a cross-domain Few-Shot Learning framework, designed to enhance model performance through pre-training on tweets containing no explicit labels for hate speech. To refine the model, we integrated task-specific fine-tuning with an uncertainty-aware inference mechanism. To address the sub-tasks of Abusive Attribute Classification and Locating, a classification module was added to predict uncertainty scores, which were then leveraged to generate location outcomes. To ensure uncertainty estimates were reliable, uncertainty calibration was performed. The secondary objective of this study involved Abusive Phrase Extraction. To improve the system's macro F1 score, we adjusted the uncertainty-aware inference framework to incorporate uncertainty scores from multiple layers. As a result, the system achieved a Macro F1 score of 23.8% for this task.

Atomic interferometry has recently enabled the detection of local magnetic fields with extraordinary sensitivity, establishing new limits for sensitivity in magnetometry. In this work, we analyze the sensitivity of such detection by separating contributions from both coherent and incoherent parts of the atomic wave function. We demonstrate that coherent components yield magnetometry limits surpassing previous established thresholds, whereas these previous limits remain applicable when applying atomic interferometry methods involving only the coherent part of the wave function. Additionally, we calculate the magnitude of these coherent contributions for two specific scenarios: magnetic field detection near atomic planes and fields generated by electron spin or nuclear magnetic moments.

We introduce the concept of an engineered magnetocaloric effect (MCE) within the spin-caloric cross-Mockeod of the CoFeB/MgO/InAs/CoFeB/Si heterostructure, designed to generate distinct magnetic-thermal responses for majority and minority spin carriers. This MCE tuning is achieved by manipulating the magnitude of the perpendicular anomalous Hall resistivity (AHER) and the temperature-dependent spin-orbit torque (SHE). The distinct behaviors of spin-selective MCE arise from the interplay between spin-dependent magneto-thermal voltage and spin-dependent heat currents. This mechanism enables the generation of triple sign-switching patterns in the adiabatic temperature change ($\Delta T_{ad}$) observed in the spin-selective MCE. This complex behavior is attributed to the specific dependence of spin-dependent spin Hall angle and spin diffusion length on temperature. This engineered spin-selective MCE mechanism offers a robust foundation for advanced spin-thermal device engineering.

Various gap models have been utilized to simulate the propagation of light through disordered dielectric waveguides, yet these models exhibit significant inaccuracies when gap dimensions approach the order of the wavelength. This study introduces an effective gap width approach that significantly improves predictions when optical mode characteristics are governed by both core and cladding forces. Unlike traditional local models that rely solely on geometric core parameters, this method incorporates local mode properties derived from a standard effective index model. By determining a revised effective gap width based on propagation constants, the approach calculates a "force-weighted" average of the optical field's confinement within the waveguide center and its surrounding cladding environment. Although highly accurate, this model functions as a "black box" that offers limited physical insight compared to other formulations. In direct contrast, the extensive analytical formulae derived to validate the analytical arguments supporting our effective gap width concept provide a robust theoretical foundation while explicitly enhancing predictive accuracy.

Although Coq and the Calculus of Consistories (CoC), developed by Gérard Huet in the 1980s, represent pillars of 21st-century type theory and dependently structured programming, scholarly attention to their historical evolution has remained limited. Coq's design addresses core concerns in 1980s type theory, notably dependent types, a sound proof assistant architecture, and a viable programming framework, all underpinned by the type-dependent lambda-calculus (CoC). This project undertakes a thorough historical and conceptual investigation of Coq's development, tracing how its creators navigated the legacy of CoC and the evolving priorities of the proof assistant community. By examining these influences, the work aims to provide fresh insights into Coq's genealogy, illuminating previously unexplored dimensions of its design history.

Recent advancements in experimental techniques for measuring optical and microwave fields have fueled a surge of interest in emerging areas of quantum optics and electronics. However, most existing research concentrates on direct state detection, leaving intermediate filtering processes largely unexplored. This paper investigates the concept of entanglement following a partial measurement of optical fields that have interacted with various wire-typed resonators. Specifically, we examine single-photon detection scenarios within both 1121 and microwave microwave resonators, as well as multi-photon detection in the 1121 case, highlighting significant differences in how single- and multi-mode modes affect quantum states depending on whether the system is single- or multi-mode. Methodologically, we utilize the correlator approach to define Radeski and M. V. entanglement measures, as well as von-Neumann entropy, finding that single-photon detection via the Radeski-V. method increases entanglement for both resonator types, whereas multi-photon detection via the Radeski-V. method induces distinct non-markovian dynamics for single vs multi-mode systems. These concepts are framed within an experimental context featuring a microwave 1121.

Admixture graphs serve as a structural framework for visual and genetic analyses, facilitating the inference of historical admixture events and population splits. This process is modeled as a problem of model selection, where potential evolutionary histories are treated as competing models. We demonstrate that selecting among these models using standard Bayesian techniques encounters a fundamental obstacle: placing prior probability distributions directly on admixture graphs results in the retrieval of non-identifiable admixture proportions. To circumvent this non-identifiability, we propose estimating admixture weights within a non-parametric Bayesian setting by applying Dirichlet process priors directly to the densities of these weights. Empirical evaluations indicate that this approach effectively recovers identifiable admixture weights even in high-dimensional scenarios characterized by unidentifiability under traditional Bayesian model averaging.

We determine the leading anomalous dimensions for the twist-four, single-trace operators in large-$N_c$ type I superstring theory at order $L^{-2}$ (where $L$ represents the 't Hooft coupling) by explicitly summing the relevant single- and double-gluon bubble diagrams. Single-bubble contributions are evaluated using a single-cut single-gluon integral, whereas double-bubble terms are derived from the two-gluon integral with double Regge kinematics. These string-theory integrals are computed within a bosonic framework where one color index of a fermionic bi-fermion vertex is replaced by an index. Our findings demonstrate that double-bubble terms are non-zero and distinct from their field-theory counterparts, exhibiting dependence on both coupling constants and the fermionic vertices. This outcome contrasts with the large-$\text{SO}(9)$ superstring case, where double-bubble contributions were previously found to vanish.

Current CUDA-based GPU allocators rely on coarse-grained memory management, reserving large blocks of RAM for tasks and leaving significant resources underutilized within allocated regions. This issue is particularly pronounced in HPC and AI domains, where the combination of massive memory capacity and diverse workloads exacerbates fragmentation. We present DynaSOAr, a novel diffusion-based dynamic memory allocator for CUDA GPUs that supersedes traditional heap strategies by operating as a free-list mechanism inside these fragmented internal areas. By resolving these constraints, DynaSQL delivers better overall performance and efficiency.

This paper investigates the influence of spin-orbit coupling on magnetic adatoms or dimers situated above a superconducting substrate, utilizing the tight-binding DFT approach combined with nonequilibrium Green's function methods to explore the resulting $2\times 2$ square lattice. We focus on sulfur and tellurium within this structural configuration. Results indicate that spin-orbit coupling shifts the YSR state peaks; this effect is attributed to alterations in the local density of states around the magnetic atoms, specifically within the $2\times 2$ square lattice arrangement. Furthermore, we observe that spin-orbit coupling significantly influences the critical temperature associated with the spin-YSR transition.

A significant challenge in remote sensing involves classifying clouds, a task complicated by clouds' dynamic nature and complex temporal and spatial variations. Our research introduces a new method for classifying cloud structures in satellite images, grounded in the concept of a "dynamic profile." This profile represents clouds as the superposition of discrete structural elements, with structural dynamics driven by the discrete movement of individual components. To operationalize this, we developed a new metric called "dynamic distance" to quantify the structural changes between consecutive image frames. Leveraging these profiles, we defined four distinct cloud structure classes. Our approach was validated using a dataset of 1,000 high-resolution satellite images, with results demonstrating strong alignment against ground truth labels derived from visual inspection. Ultimately, this cloud classification framework offers enhanced insights for advancing flood monitoring and forecasting technologies.

The interaction of a negative-chirp laser pulse with a target featuring an ultra-thin, sparse low-Z layer followed by a low-Z primary layer is investigated via fully three-dimensional, laser-pulse-polarized full-scale simulations. The presence of the intermediate low-Z spacer allows the laser's electric field to penetrate and ionize atoms from the main high-Z layer, generating a dense, hot plasma. This dense, hot low-Z plasma functions as a driver for subsequent ion acceleration, a behavior that relies on the charge state of the target ions. Specifically, for negative-chirp pulses, this driver facilitates acceleration to a dense, hot state of low-Z plasma, which in turn acts as a driver for subsequent ion acceleration—a behavior contingent upon the charge state of the target ions. This process results in the ejection of protons reaching 100 MeV and fully stripped gold ions at 15 MeV per nucleon. In the case of linear polarization, the dynamics yield ejection of 100-MeV-colliding 15-MeV/A full-Zn ions at full-Zn. Additionally, the formation of a dense, hot low-Z driver is enhanced when employing circular polarization.

We report on the detection, via transit photometry, of three mini-Neptunes orbiting the K-dwarf HD 53213 (effective temperature 4990 K). These planets have masses of 4.8, 7.8, and 10.2 Earth masses, corresponding radii of 2.4, 2.7, and 3.1 Earth radii, semi-major axes of 0.050, 0.068, and 0.083 AU, and orbital periods of 13.1, 57.4, and 186.1 days. The system's stellar luminosity is 0.029 times that of the Sun, placing the planets' orbits entirely within the conservative habitable zone (0.90–1.18 AU). The outermost planet is in a 3:1 mean-motion resonance with the middle one, while the inner two are currently 3.5 sigma away from a 5:2 resonant configuration. The transit depth for the innermost planet is 33 parts per million, and the transit duration is 3.1 hours. The transit timing variations (TTVs) for the inner pair are substantial, reaching 13.5 minutes, which allows us to constrain the minimum content of the mini-Neptune's atmosphere.

This study employs *ab initio* molecular dynamics simulations to examine the behavior of interstitial carbon and nitrogen in rutile TiO$_2$ and its doped variants. The results indicate that interstitial impurities are less stable than their substitutional equivalents, where carbon and nitrogen substitute for titanium. In contrast, interstitial carbon and nitrogen are mobile, often aggregating into linear configurations. The simulation data further supports the use of experimental Raman spectra as a diagnostic tool for distinguishing between interstitial and substitutional defects within the crystal lattice.

Flavor changing neutral current (FCNC) transitions in the sector involving single quarks occur through rare pathways such as $t \bar b W^+ \bar{t} b W^-$ and $W W \bar W \bar W$. This paper examines the first process to determine if current LHC data can improve existing constraints on its flavor changing branching fraction, which are currently estimated at less than $2.5 \times 10^{-2}$ (assuming quarks behave as massless particles) or less than $2.0 \times 10^{-2}$ (assuming quarks have a 300 GeV mass). Our findings indicate that these data sets offer no observable excess over standard model background predictions for these specific final states. Consequently, utilizing the ATLAS and CMS datasets, we establish branching ratio limits of less than $3.8 \times 10^{-2}$ (at 95% confidence) for the $W \bar W$ final state and less than $3.6 \times 10^{-2}$ (at 95% confidence) for the $\bar t W$ final state. Future improvements to these bounds will require enhanced theoretical modeling of the relevant final states and the accumulation of more extensive datasets.

The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU), part of the upcoming Athena mission, will enable precise three-dimensional maps of temperature, density, and chemical composition for the intra-cluster medium (ICM). Creating such a map is essential for addressing fundamental questions regarding the origin and evolution of the high ICM temperatures and long X-ray emission timescales, particularly by examining the roles of primordial feedback mechanisms and turbulence. While the mission will allow researchers to directly observe the broad thermodynamic structure and turbulent dynamics surrounding galaxy clusters via the line-of-sight via the spectrum of the thermal bremsstrahlung continuum, this same bremsstrahlung radiation also poses a significant challenge. Specifically, instrumental requirements for X-IFU must achieve an energy resolution of approximately 2 eV in the 4–14 keV range to effectively manage spectral deconvolution challenges caused by the continuum background.

We have created a new simulation of the density structure in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a two-dimensional, time-dependent, stochastic cloud-cloud collision code. The model aligns with observational constraints regarding the Hubble flow, gas temperature, and the H I and molecular gas mass. The resulting anisotropy of the density structure is comparable to observations at scales exceeding 200 pc but appears more pronounced at smaller scales. The simulation successfully reproduces the H I and molecular gas mass anisotropy ($M_{\rm anis}/M_{\rm tot}$) found in observations, even accounting for the lack of observed spatial smoothing in molecular gas at current resolutions. Furthermore, the model generates a velocity dispersion anisotratio ($\sigma_{\rm anis}/\sigma_{\rm tot}$) consistent with data across all scales. Additionally, cloud merging within our model naturally yields a molecular size distribution ($dN/dR \propto R^{-2.5}$) consistent with findings from both the CMZ and other galactic regions. This paper introduces EyeFocusDetection, a novel approach to detecting eyes that relies solely on eye-region crops. Traditional techniques typically need whole-face images and often demand the presence of whole faces in the scene; consequently, these methods are unsuitable for scenarios where only faces are visible or in crowded environments. Additionally, existing eye-detection standards are built on outdated datasets, resulting in a lack of research into isolated eye detection. We address these challenges by releasing EyeQu, the inaugural dataset for images featuring close-up eyes. Furthermore, we propose a new, performance-driven dual-branch network tailored for high-precision eye detection. Extensive experiments confirm that this method surpasses current leading approaches on various real-world datasets and exceed all existing baselines when evaluated against the original HD-CASIA eye qu dataset.
